title: R Colors: Names, RGB/HSV, and Building a Color Chart
text:
Background
R ships with a built-in palette of named colors, returned by colors(). As of this writing (and for a long time now) it holds 657 names — things like "steelblue", "tomato3", or "gray42". This document walks through a classic script by efg (Stowers Institute) that turns that list into a printable reference chart, and along the way explains the underlying R color machinery: how names map to RGB, how RGB maps to HSV, and how to pick readable text/background combinations automatically.
The original script writes everything to a file called COLOR_CHART.pdf. Here we reproduce each piece as an inline, explained chunk so it renders directly in this document; the full original (PDF-producing) script is included as an appendix at the end for reference.


Code
# The chart layout below hard-codes 25 columns x 27 rows = 675 slots for 657 colors.
# This assumes the palette size hasn't changed between R versions.
length(colors())


[1] 657




How R represents colors
R gives you three interchangeable ways to specify a color:

By name — a string from colors(), e.g. "firebrick".
By hex code — "#FF0000", the familiar web-style RRGGBB (optionally with alpha, RRGGBBAA).
By numeric index — a legacy palette (palette()), rarely used now.

col2rgb() converts any of the first two into the underlying 0–255 RGB triplet:


Code
col2rgb("yellow")


      [,1]
red    255
green  255
blue     0


Code
col2rgb("steelblue")


      [,1]
red     70
green  130
blue   180


RGB is how the color is stored, but it is not how humans reason about color. For that, R (via rgb2hsv()) can convert to HSV — Hue, Saturation, Value — which separates what color (hue, as an angle 0–1 representing 0–360°) from how vivid (saturation) and how bright (value):


Code
rgb2hsv(col2rgb("steelblue"))


       [,1]
h 0.5757576
s 0.6111111
v 0.7058824


Sorting colors by hue-then-saturation-then-value is what makes the second chart below (“sorted by hue”) group visually similar colors together, instead of the arbitrary alphabetical-ish order colors() returns them in.


Choosing readable text color: a contrast heuristic
Rectangles need a label (the color’s name and index) drawn on top of them. White text on "yellow" is unreadable; black text on "navy" is unreadable. The script uses a cheap luminance heuristic: average the R, G, and B channels, and if that average is above the midpoint (127.5), the background is “light” so use black text; otherwise use white text.


Code
SetTextContrastColor <- function(color) {
  ifelse(mean(col2rgb(color)) > 127, "black", "white")
}

SetTextContrastColor("white")


[1] "black"


Code
SetTextContrastColor("black")


[1] "white"


Code
SetTextContrastColor("red")


[1] "white"


Code
SetTextContrastColor("yellow")


[1] "black"


This is a simplification — perceptual luminance weights green much more heavily than blue (roughly 0.299*R + 0.587*G + 0.114*B), so a plain channel average can misjudge some saturated blues or reds. It’s good enough for a quick reference chart, though, which is the point here.
We precompute the contrast color for every entry in colors() once, so the plotting loops below can just look it up instead of recomputing it per rectangle:


Code
TextContrastColor <- unlist(lapply(colors(), SetTextContrastColor))
table(TextContrastColor)


TextContrastColor
black white 
  416   241 




Chart 1a: colors in index order
The simplest chart just walks colors() in the order R returns it, laying out 25 colors per row. Each rectangle is drawn with rect(), positioned by its row/column, filled with the color itself, and labeled with its numeric index (SetTextContrastColor decides whether that label is black or white).


Code
colCount <- 25  # number of rectangles per row
rowCount <- ceiling(length(colors()) / colCount)

oldpar <- par(mar = c(1, 1, 2, 1))

plot(c(1, colCount), c(0, rowCount), type = "n", ylab = "", xlab = "",
     axes = FALSE, ylim = c(rowCount, 0))
title("R colors (index order)")

for (j in 0:(rowCount - 1)) {
  base <- j * colCount
  remaining <- length(colors()) - base
  RowSize <- ifelse(remaining < colCount, remaining, colCount)
  rect((1:RowSize) - 0.5, j - 0.5, (1:RowSize) + 0.5, j + 0.5,
       border = "black", col = colors()[base + (1:RowSize)])
  text((1:RowSize), j, paste(base + (1:RowSize)), cex = 0.7,
       col = TextContrastColor[base + (1:RowSize)])
}









Code
par(oldpar)


Notice how little visual structure there is: R’s colors() order is alphabetical by name (with numbered variants like "blue1".."blue4" interleaved), not by appearance, so neighboring cells jump around the color wheel.


Chart 1b: colors sorted by hue, saturation, value
To get a chart that actually reads as a gradient, we convert every color to HSV and sort by hue first, then saturation, then value. order() gives us the permutation of indices that achieves that sort, and we index into colors() with it.


Code
RGBColors <- col2rgb(colors())
HSVColors <- rgb2hsv(RGBColors[1, ], RGBColors[2, ], RGBColors[3, ], maxColorValue = 255)
HueOrder <- order(HSVColors[1, ], HSVColors[2, ], HSVColors[3, ])

oldpar <- par(mar = c(1, 1, 2, 1))

plot(0, type = "n", ylab = "", xlab = "", axes = FALSE,
     ylim = c(rowCount, 0), xlim = c(1, colCount))
title("R colors -- sorted by hue, saturation, value")

for (j in 0:(rowCount - 1)) {
  for (i in 1:colCount) {
    k <- j * colCount + i
    if (k <= length(colors())) {
      rect(i - 0.5, j - 0.5, i + 0.5, j + 0.5,
           border = "black", col = colors()[HueOrder[k]])
      text(i, j, paste(HueOrder[k]), cex = 0.7,
           col = TextContrastColor[HueOrder[k]])
    }
  }
}









Code
par(oldpar)


The label in each cell is still the original index into colors() — so you can look up a color visually here, then use that number (or better, colors()[index]) to reference it by name in code.


Getting a color’s hex and decimal RGB
For a reference sheet you usually want the exact hex code (for CSS/HTML/design tools) alongside the decimal RGB triplet (for R/plotting code). sprintf() builds both from col2rgb()’s output in one line:


Code
GetColorHexAndDecimal <- function(color) {
  c <- col2rgb(color)
  sprintf("#%02X%02X%02X %3d %3d %3d", c[1], c[2], c[3], c[1], c[2], c[3])
}

GetColorHexAndDecimal("yellow")


[1] "#FFFF00 255 255   0"


Code
GetColorHexAndDecimal("steelblue")


[1] "#4682B4  70 130 180"




Chart 2: paginated detail sheet (name + hex + decimal)
The final part of the original script produces a multi-page listing: two columns of 50 colors each per page, each row showing a filled swatch, the color’s index, its name, and its hex/decimal RGB (in a monospace font so the numbers align). Below is a single representative page reproduced inline; the appendix has the full paging loop that generates every page (this is what the original script writes across the multi-page PDF).


Code
index <- paste(1:length(colors()))
HexAndDec <- unlist(lapply(colors(), GetColorHexAndDecimal))
PerColumn <- 50
PerPage <- 2 * PerColumn

page <- 1
oldpar <- par(mar = c(1, 1, 1, 1))

plot(0, type = "n", ylab = "", xlab = "", axes = FALSE,
     ylim = c(PerColumn, 0), xlim = c(0, 1))
title("R colors")
mtext(paste("page", page), side = 1, adj = 1, line = -1)

base <- PerPage * (page - 1)

# Column 1
remaining <- length(colors()) - base
ColumnSize <- ifelse(remaining < PerColumn, remaining, PerColumn)
rect(0.00, 0:(ColumnSize - 1), 0.49, 1:ColumnSize,
     border = "black", col = colors()[(base + 1):(base + ColumnSize)])
text(0.045, 0.45 + (0:(ColumnSize - 1)), adj = 1, index[(base + 1):(base + ColumnSize)],
     cex = 0.6, col = TextContrastColor[(base + 1):(base + ColumnSize)])
text(0.06, 0.45 + (0:(ColumnSize - 1)), adj = 0, colors()[(base + 1):(base + ColumnSize)],
     cex = 0.6, col = TextContrastColor[(base + 1):(base + ColumnSize)])
save <- par(family = "mono")
text(0.25, 0.45 + (0:(ColumnSize - 1)), adj = 0, HexAndDec[(base + 1):(base + ColumnSize)],
     cex = 0.6, col = TextContrastColor[(base + 1):(base + ColumnSize)])
par(save)

# Column 2
if (remaining > PerColumn) {
  remaining2 <- remaining - PerColumn
  ColumnSize2 <- ifelse(remaining2 < PerColumn, remaining2, PerColumn)
  rect(0.51, 0:(ColumnSize2 - 1), 1.00, 1:ColumnSize2,
       border = "black", col = colors()[(base + PerColumn + 1):(base + PerColumn + ColumnSize2)])
  text(0.545, 0.45 + (0:(ColumnSize2 - 1)), adj = 1,
       index[(base + PerColumn + 1):(base + PerColumn + ColumnSize2)],
       cex = 0.6, col = TextContrastColor[(base + PerColumn + 1):(base + PerColumn + ColumnSize2)])
  text(0.56, 0.45 + (0:(ColumnSize2 - 1)), adj = 0,
       colors()[(base + PerColumn + 1):(base + PerColumn + ColumnSize2)],
       cex = 0.6, col = TextContrastColor[(base + PerColumn + 1):(base + PerColumn + ColumnSize2)])
  save <- par(family = "mono")
  text(0.75, 0.45 + (0:(ColumnSize2 - 1)), adj = 0,
       HexAndDec[(base + PerColumn + 1):(base + PerColumn + ColumnSize2)],
       cex = 0.6, col = TextContrastColor[(base + PerColumn + 1):(base + PerColumn + ColumnSize2)])
  par(save)
}









Code
par(oldpar)


To generate every page (not just page 1) and get the full multi-page reference sheet, wrap that same block in a loop over page in 1:ceiling(length(colors()) / PerPage) and, when knitting, either emit one PDF page per iteration or (for HTML) let each iteration produce its own plot — see the appendix for the loop as written in the original script.


Takeaways

colors() is R’s built-in named palette (657 entries); col2rgb() and rgb2hsv() convert between name/hex, RGB, and HSV representations.
Sorting by HSV hue (not the default alphabetical order) is what makes a color chart visually navigable.
A simple average-of-channels test is a cheap-but-imperfect way to auto-pick readable black/white text on an arbitrary background color.
sprintf("#%02X%02X%02X ...") is the idiomatic way to format an RGB triplet as both hex and decimal in one string.



Appendix: original script (writes COLOR_CHART.pdf)


Code
# efg, Stowers Institute for Medical Research
# efg's Research Notes: http://research.stowers-institute.org/efg/R/Color/Chart 6 July 2004. Modified 23 May 2005.
pdf("COLOR_CHART.pdf", width = 10, height = 10)
# save to reset at end
oldparameters <- par(mar = c(1, 1, 2, 1), mfrow = c(2, 1))
# Be cautious in case definition of "colors" changes. Use some hard-coded constants since this is not expected to change.
stopifnot(length(colors()) == 657)
# 0. Setup
SetTextContrastColor <- function(color) {ifelse(mean(col2rgb(color)) > 127, "black", "white")}
TextContrastColor <- unlist(lapply(colors(), SetTextContrastColor))
# 1a. Plot matrix of R colors, in index order, 25 per row.
colCount <- 25
rowCount <- 27
plot(c(1, colCount), c(0, rowCount), type = "n", ylab = "", xlab = "", axes = FALSE, ylim = c(rowCount, 0))
title("R colors")
mtext("http://research.stowers-institute.org/efg/R/Color/Chart", cex = 0.6)
for (j in 0:(rowCount - 1)) {
  base <- j * colCount
  remaining <- length(colors()) - base
  RowSize <- ifelse(remaining < colCount, remaining, colCount)
  rect((1:RowSize) - 0.5, j - 0.5, (1:RowSize) + 0.5, j + 0.5, border = "black", col = colors()[base + (1:RowSize)])
  text((1:RowSize), j, paste(base + (1:RowSize)), cex = 0.7, col = TextContrastColor[base + (1:RowSize)])
}
# 1b. Plot matrix of R colors, in "hue" order, 25 per row.
RGBColors <- col2rgb(colors()[1:length(colors())])
HSVColors <- rgb2hsv(RGBColors[1, ], RGBColors[2, ], RGBColors[3, ], maxColorValue = 255)
HueOrder <- order(HSVColors[1, ], HSVColors[2, ], HSVColors[3, ])
plot(0, type = "n", ylab = "", xlab = "", axes = FALSE, ylim = c(rowCount, 0), xlim = c(1, colCount))
title("R colors -- Sorted by Hue, Saturation, Value")
for (j in 0:(rowCount - 1)) {
  for (i in 1:colCount) {
    k <- j * colCount + i
    if (k <= length(colors())) {
      rect(i - 0.5, j - 0.5, i + 0.5, j + 0.5, border = "black", col = colors()[HueOrder[k]])
      text(i, j, paste(HueOrder[k]), cex = 0.7, col = TextContrastColor[HueOrder[k]])
    }
  }
}
# 2. Create 7-page color chart showing rectangle block of color, along with index, color name, and RGB constants in hex and decimal.
GetColorHexAndDecimal <- function(color) {
  c <- col2rgb(color)
  sprintf("#%02X%02X%02X %3d %3d %3d", c[1], c[2], c[3], c[1], c[2], c[3])
}
par(oldparameters)
oldparameters <- par(mar = c(1, 1, 1, 1))
index <- paste(1:length(colors()))
HexAndDec <- unlist(lapply(colors(), GetColorHexAndDecimal))
PerColumn <- 50
PerPage <- 2 * PerColumn
for (page in 1:(trunc(length(colors()) + (PerPage - 1)) / PerPage)) {
  plot(0, type = "n", ylab = "", xlab = "", axes = FALSE, ylim = c(PerColumn, 0), xlim = c(0, 1))
  title("R colors")
  mtext(paste("page ", page), SOUTH <- 1, adj = 1, line = -1)
  base <- PerPage * (page - 1)
  # Column 1
  remaining <- length(colors()) - base
  ColumnSize <- ifelse(remaining < PerColumn, remaining, PerColumn)
  rect(0.00, 0:(ColumnSize - 1), 0.49, 1:ColumnSize, border = "black", col = colors()[(base + 1):(base + ColumnSize)])
  text(0.045, 0.45 + (0:(ColumnSize - 1)), adj = 1, index[(base + 1):(base + ColumnSize)], cex = 0.6, col = TextContrastColor[(base + 1):(base + ColumnSize)])
  text(0.06, 0.45 + (0:(ColumnSize - 1)), adj = 0, colors()[(base + 1):(base + ColumnSize)], cex = 0.6, col = TextContrastColor[(base + 1):(base + ColumnSize)])
  save <- par(family = "mono")
  text(0.25, 0.45 + (0:(ColumnSize - 1)), adj = 0, HexAndDec[(base + 1):(base + ColumnSize)], cex = 0.6, col = TextContrastColor[(base + 1):(base + ColumnSize)])
  par(save)
  # Column 2
  if (remaining > PerColumn) {
    remaining <- remaining - PerColumn
    ColumnSize <- ifelse(remaining < PerColumn, remaining, PerColumn)
    rect(0.51, 0:(ColumnSize - 1), 1.00, 1:ColumnSize, border = "black", col = colors()[(base + PerColumn + 1):(base + PerColumn + ColumnSize)])
    text(0.545, 0.45 + (0:(ColumnSize - 1)), adj = 1, index[(base + PerColumn + 1):(base + PerColumn + ColumnSize)], cex = 0.6, col = TextContrastColor[(base + PerColumn + 1):(base + PerColumn + ColumnSize)])
    text(0.56, 0.45 + (0:(ColumnSize - 1)), adj = 0, colors()[(base + PerColumn + 1):(base + PerColumn + ColumnSize)], cex = 0.6, col = TextContrastColor[(base + PerColumn + 1):(base + PerColumn + ColumnSize)])
    save <- par(family = "mono")
    text(0.75, 0.45 + (0:(ColumnSize - 1)), adj = 0, HexAndDec[(base + PerColumn + 1):(base + PerColumn + ColumnSize)], cex = 0.6, col = TextContrastColor[(base + PerColumn + 1):(base + PerColumn + ColumnSize)])
    par(save)
  }
}
par(oldparameters)

1. Find the station

title: Airport Weather Analysis with NOAA ISD
text:
2. Download hourly ISD data
rnoaa::isd() replaces the old wget + FTP workflow. It downloads, decompresses, and parses the ISD binary format automatically. Each call fetches one year; a loop collects all years into a list.


Code
years     <- 2001:2026
data_list <- list()

for (yr in years) {
  tryCatch({
    d <- rnoaa::isd(usaf = usaf, wban = wban, year = yr, progress = FALSE)
    data_list[[as.character(yr)]] <- d
    message("  downloaded ", yr, " (", nrow(d), " rows)")
  }, error = function(e) message("  skip ", yr, ": ", conditionMessage(e)))
}

df_raw <- bind_rows(data_list)
message("Total rows: ", nrow(df_raw))



Years where data are unavailable are silently skipped by tryCatch. 2026 data may be partial depending on when you run this.

title: Airport Weather Analysis with NOAA ISD
section: 3. Clean: sentinel values and date parsing
text:
3. Clean: sentinel values and date parsing

Why sentinel values matter
NOAA ISD encodes missing measurements as 9999 in the raw file. After dividing by 10 (ISD stores all values as tenths of the unit), missing temperature becomes 999.9°C — a physically impossible value that will corrupt any aggregate (mean, max, min) if not removed.


Code
df_data <- df_raw |>
  mutate(
    date     = as.Date(date, format = "%Y%m%d"),   # isd() returns "YYYYMMDD" strings
    temp     = as.numeric(temperature) / 10,
    dew      = as.numeric(temperature_dewpoint) / 10,
    wind_spd = as.numeric(wind_speed) / 10,
    slp      = as.numeric(air_pressure) / 10
  ) |>
  mutate(across(c(temp, dew, wind_spd, slp),
                ~ ifelse(. > 900 | . < -200, NA, .))) |>
  filter(!is.na(date))

df_data[df_data == 999.9] <- NA          # catch any remaining sentinels
df_data$month <- sub("-\\d{2}$", "", df_data$date)   # "YYYY-MM" column


Two-pass sentinel removal:

ifelse(. > 900 | . < -200, NA, .) — catches the scaled sentinels immediately after division
df_data[df_data == 999.9] <- NA — safety net for any that slipped through

title: Airport Weather Analysis with NOAA ISD
text:
4. Daily and monthly aggregates
plyr::ddply with numcolwise applies a function (here max or min) to every numeric column, grouped by date or month. Columns are then renamed with _max / _min suffixes before merging.


Code
daily_max <- plyr::ddply(df_data, "date",  plyr::numcolwise(max, na.rm = TRUE))
daily_min <- plyr::ddply(df_data, "date",  plyr::numcolwise(min, na.rm = TRUE))
month_max <- plyr::ddply(df_data, "month", plyr::numcolwise(max, na.rm = TRUE))
month_min <- plyr::ddply(df_data, "month", plyr::numcolwise(min, na.rm = TRUE))

names(daily_max)[2:length(daily_max)] <- paste0(names(daily_max)[2:length(daily_max)], "_max")
names(daily_min)[2:length(daily_min)] <- paste0(names(daily_min)[2:length(daily_min)], "_min")
names(month_max)[2:length(month_max)] <- paste0(names(month_max)[2:length(month_max)], "_max")
names(month_min)[2:length(month_min)] <- paste0(names(month_min)[2:length(month_min)], "_min")

daily <- merge(daily_max, daily_min)
month <- merge(month_max, month_min)

daily$date       <- as.Date(daily$date)
month$month_date <- as.Date(paste0(month$month, "-01"))
month            <- month[order(month$month_date), ]

title: Airport Weather Analysis with NOAA ISD
text:
5. Plots

Daily temperature ribbon
geom_ribbon fills the area between the daily min and max. The fill colour is mapped to temp_max through a diverging gradient — cold days are blue, hot days are red.


Code
plot_daily <- ggplot(daily, aes(x = date)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = temp_min, ymax = temp_max, fill = temp_max), alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_fill_gradientn(
    colours = c("#2166ac","#74add1","#fee090","#f46d43","#a50026"),
    name    = "Max °C"
  ) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "1 year", date_labels = "%Y") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "white", linewidth = 0.4, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(
    title    = str_aes(station),
    subtitle = "Daily temperature range",
    x        = NULL, y = "Temperature (°C)",
    caption  = "Source: NOAA ISD via rnoaa"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
  theme(
    plot.background    = element_rect(fill = "white", color = NA),
    axis.text.x        = element_text(angle = 90, vjust = 0.5, hjust = 1),
    panel.grid.minor.x = element_blank()
  )

plot_daily











Monthly ribbon
Aggregating to monthly level removes the noise and makes the seasonal pattern clearer. The max temperature gets a coloured gradient line; the min stays white.


Code
plot_monthly <- ggplot(month, aes(x = month_date)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = temp_min, ymax = temp_max), fill = "#74add1", alpha = 0.45) +
  geom_line(aes(y = temp_max, color = temp_max), linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_line(aes(y = temp_min), color = "white", linewidth = 0.6, alpha = 0.8) +
  scale_color_gradientn(
    colours = c("#2166ac","#74add1","#fee090","#f46d43","#a50026"),
    name    = "Max °C"
  ) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "1 year", date_labels = "%Y") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "white", linewidth = 0.4, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(
    title    = str_aes(station),
    subtitle = "Monthly temperature range",
    x        = NULL, y = "Temperature (°C)",
    caption  = "Source: NOAA ISD via rnoaa"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
  theme(
    plot.background    = element_rect(fill = "white", color = NA),
    axis.text.x        = element_text(angle = 90, vjust = 0.5, hjust = 1),
    panel.grid.minor.x = element_blank()
  )

plot_monthly











Heatmaps
A calendar heatmap puts year on the x-axis and month on the y-axis, with temperature encoded as fill colour. This format is ideal for spotting anomalies — an unusually hot August or a cold February stands out immediately.

title: Airport Weather Analysis with NOAA ISD
text:
6. Seasonal decomposition
decompose() splits a time series into three additive components:

Trend — the long-term direction (is the station getting warmer?)
Seasonal — the repeating annual cycle (summer peaks, winter troughs)
Random — what’s left after removing trend and seasonal (unusual events, measurement noise)

The frequency = 365 tells R the series repeats annually. yday() sets the correct starting position within the first year.


Code
ts_temp <- ts(
  daily$temp_max,
  frequency = 365,
  start     = c(year(min(daily$date)), yday(min(daily$date)))
)

fit <- decompose(ts_temp)

autoplot(fit) +
  labs(title = paste("Seasonal decomposition —", str_aes(station), "daily max")) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10)










Reading the decomposition: If the trend panel slopes upward over 20+ years, that is a local warming signal. The random panel should look like white noise — large spikes indicate extreme weather events.

text: Attribution: This document is a modification of original work by hrbrmstr (Bob Rudis). The visualizations have been updated to use the most recent NASA GISS surface temperature data and adapted with additional chart types.

title: NASA GISS Global Temperature Anomaly
text:
Load Data


Code
library(highcharter)

df_nasa <- read.csv(
  "https://data.giss.nasa.gov/gistemp/tabledata_v4/GLB.Ts+dSST.csv",
  header = TRUE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE, na.strings = "***", skip = 1
)

dfm <- df_nasa <- df_nasa[, c("Year", "Jan", "Feb", "Mar", "Apr", "May", "Jun",
                               "Jul", "Aug", "Sep", "Oct", "Nov", "Dec")]

dfma <- data.frame(
  Year   = df_nasa$Year,
  lower  = apply(dfm[, 2:length(dfm)], 1, min, na.rm = TRUE),
  upper  = apply(dfm[, 2:length(dfm)], 1, max, na.rm = TRUE),
  decade = paste0(substr(df_nasa$Year, 1, 3), 0)
)

dfr     <- reshape::melt(df_nasa, id.vars = "Year", variable_name = "month")
df_nasa <- merge(dfr, dfma, sort = FALSE)
df_nasa$month <- as.character(df_nasa$month)
df_nasa$year_mon <- paste0(
  df_nasa$Year, "-",
  stringr::str_pad(
    sapply(df_nasa$month, function(x) grep(paste("(?i)", x, sep = ""), month.abb)),
    2, pad = "0"
  ),
  "-01"
)
names(df_nasa) <- tolower(names(df_nasa))
df_nasa <- df_nasa[, c("year_mon", "value", "lower", "upper", "year", "decade", "month")]
df_nasa$decade <- as.numeric(df_nasa$decade)
df <- df_nasa[order(df_nasa$year_mon), ]

caption_text <- "Temperature deviation (°C) from the 1951–1980 baseline, combining land surface and ocean measurements (1880–2026). Negative values indicate cooler periods; positive values indicate warming. Recent years (2023–2024) exceed +1.2°C, approaching the Paris Agreement 1.5°C threshold. Source: NASA GISS Surface Temperature Analysis (GISTEMP v4)."

title: NASA GISS Global Temperature Anomaly
text:
Prepare Series


Code
df <- dplyr::mutate(df,
  date    = lubridate::ymd(year_mon),
  tmpstmp = datetime_to_timestamp(date),
  year    = lubridate::year(date),
  month   = lubridate::month(date, label = TRUE),
  unite   = colorize(value, viridis::viridis(10, option = "B")),
  unite   = hex_to_rgba(unite, 0.65)
)

dfcolyrs <- df %>%
  dplyr::group_by(year) %>%
  dplyr::summarise(value = median(value)) %>%
  dplyr::ungroup() %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    color_y = colorize(value, viridis::viridis(10, option = "B")),
    color_y = hex_to_rgba(color_y, 0.65)
  ) %>%
  dplyr::select(-value)

df <- dplyr::left_join(df, dfcolyrs, by = "year")

lsseries <- df %>%
  dplyr::group_by(year) %>%
  dplyr::do(data = .$value, color = dplyr::first(.$color_y)) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(name = year) %>%
  list_parse()

title: Same Crisis, Different Endings: Greece and the Euro Crisis Countries
text:
Between 2010 and 2013 six euro countries ran into deep trouble: Greece, Ireland, Portugal, Spain, Cyprus and Italy. Five of them needed rescue loans from the other euro countries, and all six went through years of cuts and lost jobs. They started from the same crisis, but they did not end up in the same place: in 2024 the average person in Ireland produced almost twice as much as in 2008, while in Greece it was still less than in 2008.
This data story compares the six countries, in plain words, on:

borrowing — how much more each country bought from abroad than it sold, before the crisis,
income — how much the country produces per person,
jobs — how many people who want work cannot find it,
investment — what the country spends on its future,
exports — how much it sells to the rest of the world,
people — whether its population grew or shrank.

Greece is in red throughout and the other five in gray. It follows on from Greece Since 2000, which tells the Greek story on its own. All the data comes from golemworldbank, an R package and Shiny app for exploring World Bank indicators; the page carries its own copy of the data for these six countries and of the one function it uses, so it runs without installing anything from GitHub.

exports — how much it sells to the rest of the world,
people — whether its population grew or shrank.

Greece is in red throughout and the other five in gray. It follows on from Greece Since 2000, which tells the Greek story on its own. All the data comes from golemworldbank, an R package and Shiny app for exploring World Bank indicators; the page carries its own copy of the data for these six countries and of the one function it uses, so it runs without installing anything from GitHub.

title: Same Crisis, Different Endings: Greece and the Euro Crisis Countries
text:
Packages


Code
# install.packages(c("dplyr", "tidyr", "plotly"))
# The data and indicator_change() come from golemworldbank, copied next to this page:
# R/code_golemworldbank.R (sourced above) and R/mfi_euro_crisis.rds. For every country,
# install golemworldbank itself; its data is in Git LFS, so install it from a clone
# (install_github() can download LFS pointer files instead of the data):
#   git lfs install
#   git clone https://github.com/sedzinfo/golemworldbank.git
# then in R:
#   devtools::install_local("golemworldbank")

library(dplyr)
library(plotly)          # interactive charts

title: Same Crisis, Different Endings: Greece and the Euro Crisis Countries
text:
The data
golemworldbank ships the World Bank’s World Development Indicators as one long table, mfi: one row per country, indicator and year. R/mfi_euro_crisis.rds holds its rows for the six countries from 2000 onwards, every indicator. We keep the indicators this story needs, each with a short name:


Code
# golemworldbank's mfi, six countries from 2000 (with the package installed, its mfi has every country)
mfi <- readRDS(paste0(directory, "R/mfi_euro_crisis.rds"))

countries <- c("Greece", "Ireland", "Portugal", "Spain", "Cyprus", "Italy")
last_year <- 2024   # the latest year with complete numbers: 2025 is still incomplete
indicators <- c(
  income             = "GDP per capita (constant 2015 US$)",
  income_gni         = "GNI per capita (constant 2015 US$)",
  unemployment       = "Unemployment, total (% of total labor force) (modeled ILO estimate)",
  youth_unemployment = "Unemployment, youth total (% of total labor force ages 15-24) (modeled ILO estimate)",
  investment         = "Gross fixed capital formation (% of GDP)",
  current_account    = "Current account balance (% of GDP)",
  exports            = "Exports of goods and services (% of GDP)",
  population         = "Population, total"
)

df_peers <- mfi %>%
  filter(`Country Name` %in% countries, `Indicator Name` %in% indicators) %>%
  mutate(country = `Country Name`,
         year    = as.numeric(as.character(Year)),
         measure = names(indicators)[match(`Indicator Name`, indicators)]) %>%
  select(country, measure, year, value) %>%
  arrange(country, measure, year)

head(df_peers, 12)


   country         measure year      value
1   Cyprus current_account 2000  -4.887475
2   Cyprus current_account 2001  -3.099168
3   Cyprus current_account 2002  -3.320125
4   Cyprus current_account 2003  -2.007671
5   Cyprus current_account 2004  -4.773275
6   Cyprus current_account 2005  -5.266826
7   Cyprus current_account 2006  -6.367948
8   Cyprus current_account 2007  -7.636691
9   Cyprus current_account 2008 -14.385541
10  Cyprus current_account 2009  -6.670743
11  Cyprus current_account 2010 -10.762276
12  Cyprus current_account 2011  -2.093436


Each row is one country, one indicator, one year:







Column
Description




country
Country name


measure
Short name of the indicator (the names of indicators above)


year
Year of observation


value
The World Bank’s value for that country and year



A few of these need a word of explanation:

Income (GDP per person) is the value of everything a country produces in a year, divided by the number of people who live there, in US dollars with price rises removed, so that years can be compared fairly. It is a rough measure of how well off the average person is.
Borrowing from abroad (the current account) is what a country earns from the rest of the world minus what it pays to it, as a share of everything it produces. A minus means it bought more than it sold and borrowed to pay the difference.
Investment is the money spent on things that help a country earn more later: new buildings, factories, machines, roads and equipment, as a share of everything the economy produces.

Every chart shades the euro crisis (2008 to 2013) and COVID (2020), and writes each country’s latest value at the end of its line; labels that would overlap are moved apart and joined to their line:


Code
# a measure's value for one country and year, and the change between two values
at <- function(m, cty, y) df_peers$value[df_peers$measure == m & df_peers$country == cty & df_peers$year == y]
change_pct <- function(from, to) round((to - from) / from * 100)
big <- function(v) format(round(v), big.mark = ",")

# Greece in red, the others in gray (as in the Greek Wages and Housing races)
highlight <- "Greece"
colour_of <- function(cty) ifelse(cty == highlight, "#E74C3C", "#B3B3B3")

shocks <- list(list(from = 2008,   to = 2013,   label = "Euro crisis"),
               list(from = 2019.5, to = 2020.5, label = "COVID"))

# chart height in pixels, set on the widget itself (width stays 100% of the
# page), so the chart always fills the box it is drawn in — no scroll bars.
# Returned inside a tagList: printed straight from a chunk, a widget's height
# is overridden by the chunk's figure size; inside a tagList it is kept
# The plotly toolbar goes down the right edge, so it never covers a long title
sized <- function(p, h) {
  p <- plotly::layout(p, modebar = list(orientation = "v"))
  p$height <- h
  htmltools::tagList(p)
}

# data source as a footnote inside each chart, at the bottom of the bottom
# margin `b` (in pixels), so it lands in the same place whatever the height
source_note <- function(b) {
  list(text = "Source: World Bank, World Development Indicators, via <a href='https://github.com/sedzinfo/golemworldbank'>golemworldbank</a>",
       xref = "paper", yref = "paper", x = 1, y = 0, yshift = -(b - 22),
       xanchor = "right", yanchor = "top", showarrow = FALSE,
       font = list(size = 11, color = "gray50"))
}

# end labels: each sits right of its line's last point; labels closer than
# `gap` pixels are pushed upwards and joined to their point by a leader line.
# `per_px` is how many y units one pixel of the plot is worth
end_labels <- function(ends, per_px, unit, gap = 17) {
  o <- order(ends$value)
  y <- ends$value[o]
  for (i in seq_along(y)[-1]) y[i] <- max(y[i], y[i - 1] + gap * per_px)
  ends$label_y[o] <- y
  lapply(seq_len(nrow(ends)), function(i) {
    name <- if (ends$country[i] == highlight) paste0("<b>", ends$country[i], "</b>") else ends$country[i]
    list(x = ends$year[i], y = ends$value[i], xref = "x", yref = "y",
         ax = 24, ay = -(ends$label_y[i] - ends$value[i]) / per_px,
         showarrow = TRUE, arrowhead = 0, arrowwidth = 1, arrowcolor = "#B3B3B3",
         xanchor = "left", text = paste0(name, " ", ends$text[i]),
         font = list(size = 12, color = "gray25"))
  })
}

# one line per country, Greece drawn last so it sits on top. `index_year`
# turns each line into "that year = 100"; `ref` draws a dotted reference line
peer_chart <- function(m, title, ytitle, unit = "", index_year = NULL, ref = NULL,
                       tozero = TRUE, h = 520) {
  d <- df_peers[df_peers$measure == m & df_peers$year >= 2000 & df_peers$year <= last_year, ]
  if (!is.null(index_year)) {
    d <- d %>% group_by(country) %>%
      mutate(value = value / value[year == index_year] * 100) %>% ungroup()
  }
  fmt <- function(v) if (unit == "$") paste0("$", big(v)) else paste0(round(v, 1), unit)
  p <- plot_ly()
  for (cty in c(setdiff(countries, highlight), highlight)) {
    dc <- d[d$country == cty, ]
    p <- add_lines(p, data = dc, x = ~year, y = ~value, name = cty,
                   line = list(color = colour_of(cty), width = if (cty == highlight) 3 else 2),
                   text = paste0(cty, " · ", dc$year, "<br>", fmt(dc$value)), hoverinfo = "text")
  }
  ends <- d %>% filter(!is.na(value)) %>% group_by(country) %>% slice_max(year) %>% ungroup() %>%
    mutate(text = fmt(value))
  b <- 110
  lo <- if (tozero) min(0, d$value, na.rm = TRUE) else min(d$value, na.rm = TRUE)
  per_px <- (max(d$value, na.rm = TRUE) - lo) * 1.1 / (h - 90 - b)
  shapes <- lapply(shocks, function(s) {
    list(type = "rect", xref = "x", yref = "paper", x0 = s$from, x1 = s$to, y0 = 0, y1 = 1,
         fillcolor = "gray92", line = list(width = 0), layer = "below")
  })
  if (!is.null(ref)) {
    shapes <- c(shapes, list(list(type = "line", xref = "paper", x0 = 0, x1 = 1, y0 = ref, y1 = ref,
                                  line = list(dash = "dot", color = "gray"))))
  }
  tags <- lapply(shocks, function(s) {
    list(x = (s$from + s$to) / 2, y = 1, xref = "x", yref = "paper", yanchor = "bottom",
         text = s$label, showarrow = FALSE, font = list(size = 12, color = "gray40"))
  })
  plotly::layout(p,
    title  = list(text = title, x = 0.02, xanchor = "left", y = 0.97, yanchor = "top"),
    margin = list(t = 90, r = 150, b = b),
    xaxis  = list(title = "", tickangle = -90, range = c(1999.5, max(d$year) + 0.5)),
    yaxis  = list(title = ytitle, ticksuffix = if (unit == "%") "%" else "",
                  rangemode = if (tozero) "tozero" else "normal"),
    showlegend = FALSE,
    shapes = shapes,
    annotations = c(tags, end_labels(ends, per_px, unit), list(source_note(b))),
    font   = list(size = 13, color = "gray25")) %>%
    sized(h)
}

# one bar per country, largest at the top, Greece in red; a negative bar
# carries its value inside, where it cannot run into the country names
ranked_bars <- function(values, title, h = 380) {
  d <- data.frame(country = names(values), value = unname(values))
  d <- d[order(d$value), ]
  b <- 80
  plot_ly(d, x = ~value, y = ~factor(country, levels = country), type = "bar", orientation = "h",
          marker = list(color = colour_of(d$country)),
          # rounding first (+ 0 turns -0 into 0) so -0.3 reads "+0%", never "-0%"
          text = sprintf("%+.0f%%", round(d$value) + 0),
          textposition = ifelse(d$value < 0, "inside", "outside"),
          textfont = list(color = ifelse(d$value < 0, "white", "gray25")), cliponaxis = FALSE,
          hovertext = paste0(d$country, ": ", sprintf("%+.1f%%", d$value)), hoverinfo = "text") %>%
    plotly::layout(
      title  = list(text = title, x = 0.02, xanchor = "left", y = 0.95, yanchor = "top"),
      margin = list(t = 70, r = 60, b = b, l = 90),
      xaxis  = list(title = "", ticksuffix = "%", zeroline = TRUE, zerolinecolor = "gray"),
      yaxis  = list(title = ""),
      annotations = list(source_note(b)),
      font   = list(size = 13, color = "gray25")) %>%
    sized(h)
}

title: Same Crisis, Different Endings: Greece and the Euro Crisis Countries
section: Before the crisis: living on borrowed money
text:
Before the crisis: living on borrowed money


Code
peer_chart("current_account",
           title  = "Buying more from abroad than selling (-) or less (+), % of the economy",
           ytitle = "% of the economy", unit = "%", ref = 0, tozero = FALSE)






In the 2000s borrowing was cheap across the euro area, and for years Greece, Portugal, Spain and Cyprus bought far more from the rest of the world than they sold, borrowing the difference. In 2008 the gap was -14.6% of everything Greece produced, -14.4% in Cyprus and -11.9% in Portugal. When the 2008 financial crisis made lenders nervous, the money stopped coming, and each country had to close the gap fast. By 2013 every one of them was close to zero. Italy borrowed little from abroad and Ireland less than the others: their problems came from a government that already owed a lot (Italy) and from banks that had lent too much on houses (Ireland).
Five of the six then needed rescue loans from the other euro countries, the International Monetary Fund or both, and in return had to cut spending and raise taxes:



Country
Rescue
Ended




Greece
three loans, 2010, 2012 and 2015
2018


Ireland
2010
2013


Portugal
2011
2014


Spain
a loan to rescue its banks, 2012
2014


Cyprus
2013, which also took money from large bank deposits
2016


Italy
none
—

title: Same Crisis, Different Endings: Greece and the Euro Crisis Countries
section: Income: from almost double to still below
text:
Income: from almost double to still below
To compare countries of different sizes, each line starts at 100 in 2008: 110 means 10% more than in 2008, 90 means 10% less.


Code
peer_chart("income", index_year = 2008, ref = 100, tozero = FALSE,
           title  = "Income per person, 2008 = 100 (price rises removed)",
           ytitle = "2008 = 100")








Code
income_change <- sapply(countries, function(cty) change_pct(at("income", cty, 2008), at("income", cty, 2024)))
ranked_bars(income_change, "Income per person: change from 2008 to 2024 (%)")






All six fell into the crisis, but they came out of it at very different speeds. By 2024 income per person was +91% in Ireland against 2008, +19% in Cyprus, +13% in Portugal, +8% in Spain and +3% in Italy. Greece is the only one still below 2008, at -10%: its fall was the deepest and its rescue the longest.

title: Same Crisis, Different Endings: Greece and the Euro Crisis Countries
section: Ireland’s numbers need a second look
text:
Ireland’s numbers need a second look
Ireland’s line shoots up from 2015 because of how GDP is counted. GDP includes everything produced in the country, and many large international companies have made Ireland the base of their business for tax reasons, so their profits count as Irish production. Much of that money goes back to the companies’ owners abroad. GNI subtracts it and counts only the income that stays with people in Ireland:


Code
d <- df_peers %>%
  filter(country == "Ireland", measure %in% c("income", "income_gni"), year <= last_year, !is.na(value)) %>%
  mutate(what = ifelse(measure == "income", "GDP per person (everything produced)", "GNI per person (income that stays)"))

p <- plot_ly(d, x = ~year, y = ~value, color = ~what, colors = c("#0082c8", "#E74C3C"),
             type = "scatter", mode = "lines+markers", marker = list(size = 7),
             text = ~paste0("Ireland · ", year, "<br>", what, ": $", big(value)), hoverinfo = "text") %>%
  plotly::layout(title  = list(text = "Ireland: what is produced and what stays (US$ per person, price rises removed)",
                               x = 0.02, xanchor = "left", y = 0.97, yanchor = "top"),
                 margin = list(t = 80, b = 150),
                 xaxis  = list(title = "", tickangle = -90),
                 yaxis  = list(title = "US$ per person", rangemode = "tozero"),
                 legend = list(orientation = "h", y = -0.2),
                 annotations = list(source_note(150)),
                 font   = list(size = 13, color = "gray25"))
sized(p, 520)






In 2024 Ireland’s GDP per person was $94,475, but its GNI per person $67,024. Even GNI is lifted by these companies, which is why Ireland’s own statistics office publishes a third measure that removes them; the World Bank does not carry it. The same companies explain the strange jumps in Ireland’s investment and borrowing lines below, such as investment of 53% of the economy in 2019, the year some of them moved patents and other intangible assets to Ireland. Ireland did recover strongly — its unemployment is among the lowest of the six — but by less than its GDP suggests.

title: Same Crisis, Different Endings: Greece and the Euro Crisis Countries
text:
Jobs: the deepest wound
The unemployment rate counts people who want a job and are looking for one, but cannot find one.


Code
peer_chart("unemployment", unit = "%",
           title  = "People looking for work who cannot find it (%)",
           ytitle = "% of people looking for work")






In 2013, 28% of people looking for work in Greece and 26% in Spain could not find a job — more than 1 in 4. Among young people (15 to 24) it was 58% in Greece and 55% in Spain, more than half. Unemployment has fallen everywhere since, but not to the same level: by 2024 it was 4.3% in Ireland and 4.9% in Cyprus, against 10% in Greece and 11.4% in Spain.

title: Same Crisis, Different Endings: Greece and the Euro Crisis Countries
text:
Investment: Greece stopped building


Code
peer_chart("investment", unit = "%",
           title  = "Investment in buildings, machines and roads (% of the economy)",
           ytitle = "% of the economy")






Investment fell in every country during the crisis. Most of them went back to around a fifth of what they produce, but Greece fell furthest — from 23% in 2008 to 12% in 2013 — and stayed there until 2019. In 2024 it was still 16%, the lowest of the six. A country that invests little for a decade has fewer new factories, machines and roads to earn from, which is one reason Greek incomes have been slowest to recover. (Ireland’s line jumps around for the reasons in the section above.)

title: Same Crisis, Different Endings: Greece and the Euro Crisis Countries
text:
Exports: everyone sells more abroad


Code
peer_chart("exports", unit = "%",
           title  = "Exports of goods and services (% of the economy)",
           ytitle = "% of the economy")








Code
exports_change <- sapply(countries, function(cty) round(at("exports", cty, 2024) - at("exports", cty, 2008)))
ranked_bars(exports_change, "Exports: change from 2008 to 2024 (percentage points of the economy)")






The one thing all six did after the crisis was to sell more to the rest of the world. Greek exports went from 23% of the economy in 2008 to 42% in 2024, Portugal’s from 31% to 46%. The bar chart shows the change in percentage points: Greece’s exports grew by 19 points of its economy. Ireland’s exports are bigger than its whole economy, and Cyprus’s almost as big, because exports count the full value of what is sold, including parts that were imported first.

title: Same Crisis, Different Endings: Greece and the Euro Crisis Countries
section: People: who stayed and who left
text:
People: who stayed and who left


Code
population_change <- sapply(countries, function(cty) change_pct(at("population", cty, 2008), at("population", cty, 2024)))
ranked_bars(population_change, "Population: change from 2008 to 2024 (%)")






During the crisis many people, often young and well educated, left to find work elsewhere. In the countries that recovered quickly, people came back and newcomers arrived: from 2008 to 2024 the population grew by 24% in Cyprus and 20% in Ireland. Greece’s shrank by 6%, also because Greek families have few children; Italy’s stayed about the same.

title: Same Crisis, Different Endings: Greece and the Euro Crisis Countries
text:
Comparing 2008 with 2024 with indicator_change()
golemworldbank’s indicator_change() compares every indicator a country has in two years — the same comparison as the app’s Change (%) tab. Running it for each country from 2008 to 2024 and keeping the indicators of this story gives one table of percentage changes:


Code
change_2008_2024 <- bind_rows(lapply(countries, function(cty) {
  res <- indicator_change(mfi, country = cty, year1 = 2008, year2 = 2024)
  both <- rbind(res$increased, res$decreased)
  both <- both[both$Indicator %in% indicators[names(indicators) != "current_account"], ]
  data.frame(measure = names(indicators)[match(both$Indicator, indicators)],
             country = cty, change = round(both$`Change %`))
}))

change_2008_2024 %>%
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = country, values_from = change) %>%
  arrange(match(measure, names(indicators))) %>%
  as.data.frame()


             measure Greece Ireland Portugal Spain Cyprus Italy
1             income    -10      91       13     8     19     3
2         income_gni     -7      70       22    10     10     4
3       unemployment     31     -37      -14     1     30    -3
4 youth_unemployment      4     -23       31     9     51    -5
5         investment    -31     -30      -11   -27    -24     0
6            exports     85      71       47    45     94    21
7         population     -6      20        1     6     24     0


Each number is the percentage change from 2008 to 2024: income -10 for Greece means 10% less than in 2008. Unemployment, investment and exports are themselves percentages, so their change is relative to the 2008 level (unemployment in Ireland going from 6.8% to 4.3% is a change of -37%). Borrowing from abroad is left out: it is a number that can be below zero, and a percentage change of a negative number, or of one that turns from a minus into a plus, has no clear meaning.

title: Same Crisis, Different Endings: Greece and the Euro Crisis Countries
text:
What the charts show


Code
snapshot <- df_peers %>%
  filter(year %in% c(2008, 2013, 2024), measure %in% c("income", "unemployment", "investment", "exports")) %>%
  mutate(value = round(value, 1)) %>%
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = country, values_from = value) %>%
  arrange(match(measure, names(indicators)), year) %>%
  as.data.frame()
snapshot


        measure year  Cyprus  Greece Ireland   Italy Portugal   Spain
1        income 2008 27449.2 23923.9 49461.2 33550.6  20014.5 27112.5
2        income 2013 22711.7 17644.9 47928.0 30330.0  18597.7 24498.6
3        income 2024 32757.5 21494.7 94475.0 34508.1  22664.0 29245.2
4  unemployment 2008     3.8     7.7     6.8     6.7      7.6    11.3
5  unemployment 2013    16.1    27.7    13.7    12.1     16.2    26.1
6  unemployment 2024     4.9    10.0     4.3     6.5      6.5    11.4
7    investment 2008    27.2    23.3    24.8    21.6     22.9    27.9
8    investment 2013    14.1    11.5    18.3    17.3     14.8    17.6
9    investment 2024    20.5    16.0    17.3    21.5     20.4    20.3
10      exports 2008    50.1    22.8    84.3    26.7     31.3    25.5

The same start: before 2008, Greece, Cyprus, Portugal and Spain bought far more from abroad than they sold and borrowed the difference. When the borrowing stopped, all of them had to cut back at once.
Different endings: from 2008 to 2024 income per person rose by 91% in Ireland (less in reality, see GNI), 19% in Cyprus, 13% in Portugal, 8% in Spain and 3% in Italy, and fell by 10% in Greece.
Jobs came back everywhere, but Greece and Spain still have the highest unemployment of the six: 10% and 11.4% in 2024, against 4.3% to 6.5% in the other four.
Investment is where Greece differs most: it has invested the least of the six every year since 2010.
Exports grew in all six — the one recipe every country followed.
People voted with their feet: the countries that recovered fastest gained population, Greece lost it.

title: Same Crisis, Different Endings: Greece and the Euro Crisis Countries
text:
Customising it

Highlight a different country


Code
highlight <- "Portugal"
peer_chart("income", index_year = 2008, ref = 100, tozero = FALSE,
           title = "Income per person, 2008 = 100", ytitle = "2008 = 100")




Add a country
R/mfi_euro_crisis.rds holds these six countries only. With golemworldbank installed (see Packages), its mfi has every country: load it instead of the file and add the country to countries.
library(golemworldbank)   # replaces mfi <- readRDS(...)
countries <- c("Greece", "Ireland", "Portugal", "Spain", "Cyprus", "Italy", "Germany")


Another pair of years


Code
recovery <- indicator_change(mfi, country = "Portugal", year1 = 2013, year2 = 2019)
head(recovery$increased)
head(recovery$decreased)

title: Recreating Hans Rosling’s Bubble Chart in R
text:
In 2006, Hans Rosling gave a TED talk that changed how people think about global development. His animated bubble chart showed 200 years of data in 4 minutes, revealing that the world is far less divided between “rich” and “poor” than most people assume.
This tutorial shows you how to recreate that chart in R using freely available packages — no API keys, no paid data, just a few lines of code.

title: Recreating Hans Rosling’s Bubble Chart in R
text:
In 2006, Hans Rosling gave a TED talk that changed how people think about global development. His animated bubble chart showed 200 years of data in 4 minutes, revealing that the world is far less divided between “rich” and “poor” than most people assume.
This tutorial shows you how to recreate that chart in R using freely available packages — no API keys, no paid data, just a few lines of code.

title: Recreating Hans Rosling’s Bubble Chart in R
text:
Packages


Code
# install.packages(c("gapminder", "ggplot2", "gganimate", "gifski", "scales"))

library(gapminder)   # the data
library(ggplot2)     # plotting
library(gganimate)   # animation
library(gifski)      # GIF renderer
library(scales)      # axis formatting

data(gapminder)

title: Recreating Hans Rosling’s Bubble Chart in R
text:
The data
The gapminder package ships with a clean, ready-to-use dataset. No downloading required.


Code
head(gapminder, 12)

12 Afghanistan Asia       2007    43.8 31889923      975.


It covers 142 countries across 5 continents, with observations every 5 years from 1952 to 2007.
Each row is one country in one year, with:



Column
Description




country
Country name


continent
Continent


year
Year (every 5 years)


lifeExp
Life expectancy at birth


pop
Population


gdpPercap
GDP per capita (inflation-adjusted USD)

title: Recreating Hans Rosling’s Bubble Chart in R
section: Building the chart step by step
text:
Building the chart step by step

Step 1 — the basic scatter
Start with a single year to get the layout right before adding animation.


Code
gapminder_2007 <- gapminder[gapminder$year == 2007, ]

ggplot(gapminder_2007,
       aes(x = gdpPercap, y = lifeExp, size = pop, color = continent)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(title = "2007", x = "GDP per capita", y = "Life expectancy") +
  theme_minimal()









Three things are already encoded: wealth (x), health (y), and population (bubble size). Continent gets color.


Step 2 — improve the axes
GDP per capita spans from ~$200 to ~$100,000. A log scale is essential — on a linear scale, poor countries are crushed into the left margin and you lose all the variation that matters.


Code
ggplot(gapminder_2007,
       aes(x = gdpPercap, y = lifeExp, size = pop, color = continent)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.75) +
  scale_x_log10(
    breaks = c(500, 1000, 2000, 5000, 10000, 50000),
    labels = label_dollar(scale_cut = cut_short_scale())
  ) +
  scale_size(range = c(2, 24), guide = "none") +
  labs(title = "2007", x = "GDP per capita (log scale)", y = "Life expectancy") +
  theme_minimal()









range = c(2, 24) in scale_size maps the smallest population to a 2px bubble and the largest (China, India) to 24px. The guide = "none" removes the size legend — it’s not readable anyway.


Step 3 — label the big ones


Code
big_countries <- c("China", "India", "United States", "Brazil", "Nigeria")

ggplot(gapminder_2007,
       aes(x = gdpPercap, y = lifeExp, size = pop, color = continent)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.75) +
  geom_text(
    data = \(d) d[d$country %in% big_countries, ],
    aes(label = country),
    size = 3.2, vjust = -1.1, show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  scale_x_log10(
    breaks = c(500, 1000, 2000, 5000, 10000, 50000),
    labels = label_dollar(scale_cut = cut_short_scale())
  ) +
  scale_size(range = c(2, 24), guide = "none") +
  labs(title = "2007", x = "GDP per capita (log scale)", y = "Life expectancy") +
  theme_minimal()











Step 4 — dark theme + colors


Code
continent_colors <- c(
  Africa   = "#E74C3C",
  Americas = "#F39C12",
  Asia     = "#3498DB",
  Europe   = "#2ECC71",
  Oceania  = "#9B59B6"
)

dark_theme <- theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    plot.background  = element_rect(fill = "#0F1923", color = NA),
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = "#0F1923", color = NA),
    panel.grid.major = element_line(color = "#1E2D3D"),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    text             = element_text(color = "white"),
    axis.text        = element_text(color = "#90A4AE"),
    legend.position  = "bottom",
    legend.text      = element_text(size = 11),
    plot.caption     = element_text(color = "#546E7A", size = 8, hjust = 1)
  )

ggplot(gapminder_2007,
       aes(x = gdpPercap, y = lifeExp, size = pop, color = continent)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.75, stroke = 0.2) +
  geom_text(
    data = \(d) d[d$country %in% big_countries, ],
    aes(label = country),
    size = 3.2, vjust = -1.1, show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  scale_x_log10(
    breaks = c(500, 1000, 2000, 5000, 10000, 50000),
    labels = label_dollar(scale_cut = cut_short_scale())
  ) +
  scale_size(range = c(2, 24), guide = "none") +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = continent_colors,
    guide  = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 5))
  ) +
  labs(
    title   = "2007",
    x       = "GDP per capita (log scale)",
    y       = "Life expectancy at birth",
    color   = NULL,
    caption = "Source: Gapminder  |  Bubble size = population"
  ) +
  dark_theme











Step 5 — animate it
gganimate extends ggplot2 with transition_* functions. transition_time(year) moves through the year variable. shadow_mark() leaves a faint ghost trail so you can see where countries have been.


Code
p <- ggplot(gapminder,
            aes(x = gdpPercap, y = lifeExp, size = pop, color = continent)) +

  geom_point(alpha = 0.75, stroke = 0.2) +

  geom_text(
    data = \(d) d[d$country %in% big_countries, ],
    aes(label = country),
    size = 3.2, vjust = -1.1, show.legend = FALSE
  ) +

  scale_x_log10(
    breaks = c(500, 1000, 2000, 5000, 10000, 50000),
    labels = label_dollar(scale_cut = cut_short_scale())
  ) +
  scale_size(range = c(2, 24), guide = "none") +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = continent_colors,
    guide  = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 5))
  ) +

  labs(
    title   = "{as.integer(frame_time)}",   # <-- the magic: year as title
    x       = "GDP per capita (log scale)",
    y       = "Life expectancy at birth",
    color   = NULL,
    caption = "Source: Gapminder  |  Bubble size = population"
  ) +

  dark_theme +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 54, face = "bold", hjust = 0.5)) +

  transition_time(year) +      # animate over year
  ease_aes("linear") +         # constant speed between frames
  shadow_mark(alpha = 0.06, size = 0.4)   # ghost trail

animate(p,
        nframes  = 120,
        fps      = 12,
        width    = 900,
        height   = 650,
        units    = "px",
        res      = 96,
        renderer = gifski_renderer("gapminder.gif"))










Note: rendering takes ~1–2 minutes. The GIF will appear in your working directory (getwd()).

title: Recreating Hans Rosling’s Bubble Chart in R
text:
What the chart shows

Africa (red) clusters bottom-left in 1952 — low income, low life expectancy — and moves right and up over 55 years, but more slowly than other continents.
Asia (blue) shows the most dramatic movement. South Korea, Singapore, and China all make huge leaps.
Europe (green) starts already in the upper-right and pushes further right.
The gap between rich and poor narrows dramatically — the world Rosling called “two humps” in 1952 becomes one.

title: Recreating Hans Rosling’s Bubble Chart in R
text:
Customising it

Change which countries get labels


Code
big_countries <- c("China", "India", "United States", "Germany", "Japan")




Change the speed


Code
animate(p, nframes = 60, fps = 6, ...)   # slower
animate(p, nframes = 240, fps = 24, ...) # smoother




Filter to one continent


Code
gapminder_asia <- gapminder[gapminder$continent == "Asia", ]
# then replace gapminder with gapminder_asia in the ggplot() call




Save as MP4 instead of GIF


Code
# install.packages("av")
animate(p, renderer = av_renderer("gapminder.mp4"), fps = 24, width = 1280, height = 720)

title: Greece Since 2000: Boom, Crisis and Recovery
text:
If you compare Greece in 2000 with Greece in 2020, you get a confusing picture. Both years are unusual: in 2000 Greece did not yet use the euro, and 2020 was the year COVID shut the world down. In between, Greece went through a boom, a very deep crisis and a slow recovery, and two snapshots cannot show that.
This data story follows Greece year by year, in plain words, through the World Bank’s numbers on:

income — how much the country produces per person,
jobs — how many people who want work cannot find it,
investment — what the country spends on its future,
people — who moves in and out, and how old the population is,
energy — where the electricity comes from.

All the data comes from golemworldbank, an R package and Shiny app for exploring World Bank indicators. The page carries its own copy of the Greek data and of the one function it uses, so it runs without installing anything from GitHub; install golemworldbank to do the same for any other country, or to explore the data in the app.

title: Greece Since 2000: Boom, Crisis and Recovery
text:
Packages


Code
# install.packages(c("dplyr", "tidyr", "plotly"))
# The data and indicator_change() come from golemworldbank, copied next to this page:
# R/code_golemworldbank.R (sourced above) and R/mfi_greece.rds. For every country,
# install golemworldbank itself; its data is in Git LFS, so install it from a clone
# (install_github() can download LFS pointer files instead of the data):
#   git lfs install
#   git clone https://github.com/sedzinfo/golemworldbank.git
# then in R:
#   devtools::install_local("golemworldbank")

library(dplyr)
library(plotly)          # interactive charts

title: Greece Since 2000: Boom, Crisis and Recovery
text:
The data
golemworldbank ships the World Bank’s World Development Indicators as one long table, mfi: one row per country, indicator and year. R/mfi_greece.rds holds its rows for Greece, every indicator and year. We keep the years from 2000 onwards and the indicators this story needs, each with a short name:


Code
# golemworldbank's mfi, Greece only (with the package installed, its mfi has every country)
mfi <- readRDS(paste0(directory, "R/mfi_greece.rds"))

indicators <- c(
  income             = "GDP per capita (constant 2015 US$)",
  unemployment       = "Unemployment, total (% of total labor force) (modeled ILO estimate)",
  youth_unemployment = "Unemployment, youth total (% of total labor force ages 15-24) (modeled ILO estimate)",
  investment         = "Gross fixed capital formation (% of GDP)",
  net_migration      = "Net migration",
  population         = "Population, total",
  aged_65            = "Population ages 65 and above (% of total population)",
  fertility          = "Fertility rate, total (births per woman)",
  coal               = "Electricity production from coal sources (% of total)",
  renewables         = "Renewable electricity output (% of total electricity output)",
  gas                = "Electricity production from natural gas sources (% of total)",
  tourism            = "International tourism, receipts (current US$)",
  life_expectancy    = "Life expectancy at birth, total (years)",
  internet           = "Individuals using the Internet (% of population)",
  exports            = "Exports of goods and services (% of GDP)",
  poverty            = "Poverty headcount ratio at societal poverty line (% of population)"
)

df_greece <- mfi %>%
  filter(`Country Name` == "Greece", `Indicator Name` %in% indicators) %>%
  mutate(year    = as.numeric(as.character(Year)),
         measure = names(indicators)[match(`Indicator Name`, indicators)]) %>%
  filter(year >= 2000) %>%
  select(measure, year, value) %>%
  arrange(measure, year)

head(df_greece, 12)


   measure year    value
1  aged_65 2000 17.02536
2  aged_65 2001 17.26438
3  aged_65 2002 17.53454
4  aged_65 2003 17.83265
5  aged_65 2004 18.10322
6  aged_65 2005 18.32481
7  aged_65 2006 18.48934
8  aged_65 2007 18.60483
9  aged_65 2008 18.71140
10 aged_65 2009 18.88299
11 aged_65 2010 19.15789
12 aged_65 2011 19.50739


Each row is one indicator in one year:







Column
Description




measure
Short name of the indicator (the names of indicators above)


year
Year of observation


value
The World Bank’s value for Greece in that year



Two of these need a word of explanation:

Income is the value of everything Greece produces in a year, divided by the number of people who live there, in US dollars with price rises removed, so that years can be compared fairly. It is a rough measure of how well off the average person is.
Investment is the money spent on things that help a country earn more later: new buildings, factories, machines, roads and equipment, as a share of everything the economy produces.

Every chart below shades the two shocks of the period — the debt crisis (2008 to 2013) and COVID (2020) — and writes the latest value at the end of each line:


Code
# the latest value of a measure, and its value in a given year
at <- function(m, y) df_greece$value[df_greece$measure == m & df_greece$year == y]
last_year <- function(m) max(df_greece$year[df_greece$measure == m])
latest <- function(m) at(m, last_year(m))
change_pct <- function(from, to) round((to - from) / from * 100)
big <- function(v) format(round(v), big.mark = ",")

# "$21,922" for dollars, "8.5%" for percentages
fmt <- function(v, unit) {
  if (unit == "$") paste0("$", big(v)) else paste0(round(v, 1), unit)
}

shocks <- list(list(from = 2008,   to = 2013,   label = "Debt crisis"),
               list(from = 2019.5, to = 2020.5, label = "COVID"))

# chart height in pixels, set on the widget itself (width stays 100% of the
# page), so the chart always fills the box it is drawn in — no scroll bars.
# Returned inside a tagList: printed straight from a chunk, a widget's height
# is overridden by the chunk's figure size; inside a tagList it is kept
# The plotly toolbar goes down the right edge, so it never covers a long title
sized <- function(p, h) {
  p <- plotly::layout(p, modebar = list(orientation = "v"))
  p$height <- h
  htmltools::tagList(p)
}

# title, shaded shocks, end labels and the data source in one layout() call
# (a second layout(annotations = ...) would replace the first one's). The
# source sits at the bottom of the bottom margin `b`, in pixels, so it lands
# in the same place whatever the chart's height; the x axis range is fixed,
# because plotly would otherwise widen it to make room for the end labels
finish <- function(p, title, ytitle, labels, unit = "", legend = TRUE, b = if (legend) 150 else 110) {
  shapes <- lapply(shocks, function(s) {
    list(type = "rect", xref = "x", yref = "paper", x0 = s$from, x1 = s$to, y0 = 0, y1 = 1,
         fillcolor = "gray92", line = list(width = 0), layer = "below")
  })
  tags <- lapply(shocks, function(s) {
    list(x = (s$from + s$to) / 2, y = 1, xref = "x", yref = "paper", yanchor = "bottom",
         text = s$label, showarrow = FALSE, font = list(size = 12, color = "gray40"))
  })
  source_note <- list(
    text = "Source: World Bank, World Development Indicators, via <a href='https://github.com/sedzinfo/golemworldbank'>golemworldbank</a>",
    xref = "paper", yref = "paper", x = 1, y = 0, yshift = -(b - 22),
    xanchor = "right", yanchor = "top", showarrow = FALSE,
    font = list(size = 11, color = "gray50"))
  plotly::layout(p,
    title  = list(text = title, x = 0.02, xanchor = "left", y = 0.97, yanchor = "top"),
    margin = list(t = 90, r = 130, b = b),
    xaxis  = list(title = "", tickangle = -90, range = c(1999.5, max(df_greece$year) + 0.5)),
    yaxis  = list(title = ytitle, ticksuffix = if (unit == "%") "%" else "", rangemode = "tozero"),
    legend = list(orientation = "h", y = -0.2),
    showlegend = legend,
    shapes = shapes,
    annotations = c(tags, labels, list(source_note)),
    font   = list(size = 13, color = "gray25"))
}

# one line per measure, each with its value written at the end; `nudge` lifts
# a label (in pixels) off a line it would otherwise be written over
story_chart <- function(measures, names, short, colors, title, ytitle, unit = "", h = 520,
                        nudge = rep(0, length(measures))) {
  p <- plot_ly()
  ends <- list()
  for (i in seq_along(measures)) {
    d <- df_greece[df_greece$measure == measures[i], ]
    p <- add_trace(p, data = d, x = ~year, y = ~value, name = names[i],
                   type = "scatter", mode = "lines+markers",
                   line = list(color = colors[i], width = 2),
                   marker = list(color = colors[i], size = 7),
                   text = paste0(names[i], " · ", d$year, "<br>", fmt(d$value, unit)),
                   hoverinfo = "text")
    ends[[i]] <- list(x = last_year(measures[i]), y = latest(measures[i]), xref = "x", yref = "y",
                      xanchor = "left", xshift = 8, yshift = nudge[i], showarrow = FALSE,
                      text = trimws(paste(short[i], fmt(latest(measures[i]), unit))),
                      font = list(size = 13, color = "gray25"))
  }
  finish(p, title, ytitle, ends, unit, legend = length(measures) > 1) %>% sized(h)
}

title: Greece Since 2000: Boom, Crisis and Recovery
text:
Greece at a glance


Code
peak   <- df_greece %>% filter(measure == "income", year <= 2010) %>% slice_max(value)
bottom <- df_greece %>% filter(measure == "income", year > 2008, year <= 2016) %>% slice_min(value)

p <- plot_ly(df_greece[df_greece$measure == "income", ], x = ~year, y = ~value,
             type = "scatter", mode = "lines+markers",
             line = list(color = "#0082c8", width = 2), marker = list(color = "#0082c8", size = 7),
             text = ~paste0("Greece · ", year, "<br>", fmt(value, "$"), " per person"), hoverinfo = "text")
finish(p, "Greece: how much the country produces per person (US$, price rises removed)", "US$ per person",
       labels = list(
         list(x = peak$year, y = peak$value, yshift = 10, yanchor = "bottom", showarrow = FALSE,
              text = paste0("Peak ", peak$year, ": ", fmt(peak$value, "$")), font = list(color = "gray25")),
         list(x = bottom$year, y = bottom$value, yshift = -10, yanchor = "top", showarrow = FALSE,
              text = paste0("Bottom ", bottom$year, ": ", fmt(bottom$value, "$")), font = list(color = "gray25")),
         list(x = last_year("income"), y = latest("income"), xanchor = "left", xshift = 8, showarrow = FALSE,
              text = fmt(latest("income"), "$"), font = list(color = "gray25"))),
       legend = FALSE) %>%
  sized(520)






The line has five chapters:

2000 to 2008: boom. Joining the euro made borrowing cheap for the government and for families, and money flowed in. Income per person grew by 33%. Part of that growth was paid for with borrowed money.
2008 to 2013: crisis. In late 2009 it came out that the government’s finances were far worse than it had reported. From 2010 Greece needed rescue loans from other euro countries and the International Monetary Fund, and in return it had to cut wages, pensions and public spending and raise taxes. Income per person fell by 26% in five years.
2013 to 2019: slow recovery. The economy grew again, slowly. The last rescue programme ended in 2018.
2020: COVID. Tourists stopped coming and the economy fell again.
2021 onwards: rebound. Growth returned, but in 2025 income per person was still 8% below 2008.

title: Greece Since 2000: Boom, Crisis and Recovery
section: Jobs: the deepest wound, now healing
text:
Jobs: the deepest wound, now healing
The unemployment rate counts people who want a job and are looking for one, but cannot find one.


Code
story_chart(c("unemployment", "youth_unemployment"),
            names  = c("Everyone", "Young people (15 to 24)"),
            short  = c("Everyone", "Young"),
            colors = c("#0082c8", "#E74C3C"),
            title  = "Greece: people looking for work who cannot find it (%)",
            ytitle = "% of people looking for work", unit = "%")






In 2013, 28% of people looking for work could not find a job — more than 1 in 4. Among young people it was 58%, almost 6 in 10. Since then unemployment has fallen every year, and by 2025 it was back near its level before the crisis (8.5%, against 7.7% in 2008).

title: Greece Since 2000: Boom, Crisis and Recovery
section: Investment: what has not come back
text:
Investment: what has not come back


Code
story_chart("investment", names = "Investment", short = "",
            colors = "#0082c8",
            title  = "Greece: investment in buildings, machines and roads (% of the economy)",
            ytitle = "% of the economy", unit = "%")






Before the crisis Greece invested about a quarter of what it produced. During the crisis this fell to about a tenth (11.5% in 2013) and stayed there until 2019. It is rising again (16.9% in 2025), but it is still well below where it was. A decade of low investment is one reason incomes have not fully recovered.

title: Greece Since 2000: Boom, Crisis and Recovery
text:
People: fewer and older
Net migration is the number of people who moved into the country minus the number who moved out. Blue bars mean more people arrived than left; red bars mean more people left than arrived.


Code
d <- df_greece %>%
  filter(measure == "net_migration") %>%
  mutate(color = ifelse(value >= 0, "#0082c8", "#E74C3C"),
         what  = ifelse(value >= 0, "more arrived than left", "more left than arrived"))

p <- plot_ly(d, x = ~year, y = ~value, type = "bar",
             marker = list(color = ~color),
             text = ~paste0("Greece · ", year, "<br>", big(value), " people: ", what),
             hoverinfo = "text", textposition = "none")
finish(p, "Greece: people who moved in, minus people who moved out, per year", "people per year",
       labels = list(), legend = FALSE) %>%
  sized(520)






During the crisis many people, often young and well educated, moved abroad to find work: between 2011 and 2015 about 250,000 more people left Greece than arrived. Treat the latest years with care — the World Bank’s estimates for them jump sharply from one year to the next.
At the same time, Greek families have few children: about 1.2 per woman, while about 2 are needed to keep a population steady. Together these explain why there are fewer Greeks now (10.4 million in 2025, down from 11.1 million around 2010) and why they are older: people aged 65 and over were 17% of the population in 2000 and 24% in 2025.

title: Greece Since 2000: Boom, Crisis and Recovery
text:
Energy: much less coal
Most of Greece’s electricity used to come from lignite, a cheap and dirty kind of coal. Those power stations are being closed, and solar parks, wind farms and power stations that burn natural gas have taken their place.


Code
story_chart(c("coal", "renewables", "gas"),
            names  = c("Coal", "Renewable (sun, wind, water)", "Natural gas"),
            short  = c("Coal", "Renewable", "Gas"),
            colors = c("#E74C3C", "#0082c8", "#999999"),
            title  = "Greece: where the electricity comes from (% of all electricity)",
            ytitle = "% of all electricity", unit = "%",
            nudge  = c(0, 14, 0))   # renewables stop in 2021, above the gas line






In 2000 coal made 64% of Greece’s electricity; by 2025 it made 5%. Renewable sources went from 8% to 41% (2021 is the last year the World Bank reports), and natural gas from 11% to 39%.

title: Greece Since 2000: Boom, Crisis and Recovery
text:
Comparing two years with indicator_change()
golemworldbank’s indicator_change() compares every indicator a country has in two years and splits them into those that went up and those that went down, each sorted by percentage change — the same comparison as the app’s Change (%) tab. The result depends entirely on which two years you pick. Comparing 2000 with 2020 mixes twenty years of change with one very bad year: in 2019 tourists spent $23 billion in Greece, in 2020 $6 billion, a fall of 73% in one year.
These pairs each answer one clear question:



Question
From
To




What did the boom look like?
2000
2008


How bad was the crisis?
2008
2013


How strong was the recovery?
2013
2019


Is Greece back to where it was?
2008
2024



Avoid 2020 and 2021 as end points, because COVID makes almost everything look worse than the real trend, and use 2024 as the latest year, because the 2025 numbers are still incomplete. The crisis, for example:


Code
crisis <- indicator_change(mfi, country = "Greece", year1 = 2008, year2 = 2013)
c(increased = nrow(crisis$increased), decreased = nrow(crisis$decreased))


increased decreased 
      319       474 


Code
# the indicators of this story, by their short names
headline <- function(tab) {
  tab <- tab[tab$Indicator %in% indicators, ]
  tab$Indicator <- names(indicators)[match(tab$Indicator, indicators)]
  # 3 significant digits, with thousands separators and no scientific notation
  tab[, 2:4] <- lapply(tab[, 2:4], function(x) {
    vapply(x, function(v) format(signif(v, 3), big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE), "")
  })
  tab
}

50  investment           23.3           11.5        -11.7   -50.45
170     income         23,900         17,600       -6,280   -26.25
271  fertility            1.5           1.29        -0.21   -14.00

457    tourism 17,600,000,000 17,400,000,000 -175,000,000    -0.99


Because it compares hundreds of indicators automatically, some odd ones end up at the top of the list. These ones do not mean what they seem to:

Fossil fuels “fall to 0%”. From 2017 the World Bank stopped reporting this figure for Greece, and the gap shows up as 0.
The exchange rate “falls 99.8%” between 2000 and any later year. In 2000 it was counted in drachmas, and from 2001 in euros: nothing collapsed, the currency changed.
“Children out of school” jumps 50 times. This figure moves up and down from year to year because of changes in how it is measured.
University enrolment above 100%. It counts everyone enrolled, including older students and students who stay registered for many years, and divides them by the number of people of student age.
Huge percentages on small numbers. Going from a few hundred to a few thousand is a big percentage, even when the numbers themselves are small.

title: Greece Since 2000: Boom, Crisis and Recovery
text:
What the charts show


Code
snapshot <- df_greece %>%
  filter(year %in% c(2000, 2008, 2013, 2019, 2024),
         measure %in% c("income", "unemployment", "youth_unemployment", "investment", "poverty",
                        "exports", "aged_65", "life_expectancy", "coal", "internet")) %>%
  mutate(value = round(value, 1)) %>%
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = year, values_from = value) %>%
  as.data.frame()
snapshot


              measure    2000    2008    2013    2019    2024
1             aged_65    17.0    18.7    20.3    22.1    23.9
2                coal    63.7    52.3    46.2    24.9     5.6
3             exports    24.0    22.8    30.3    39.6    42.1
4              income 18002.9 23923.9 17644.9 19216.7 21494.7
5            internet     9.1    38.2    59.9    75.7    86.3
6          investment    25.9    23.3    11.5    11.0    16.0
7     life_expectancy    77.9    79.9    81.3    81.6    81.8
8             poverty    17.6    15.0    20.4    17.0      NA
9        unemployment    11.3     7.7    27.7    17.0    10.0
10 youth_unemployment    29.0    21.6    58.5    34.8    22.4



Income: up 33% in the boom, down 26% in the crisis, and in 2025 still 8% below 2008.
Jobs: unemployment peaked at 28% in 2013 (58% for young people) and is now back near pre-crisis levels.
Investment: fell from about a quarter of the economy to about a tenth, and has only partly come back.
People: fewer (10.4 million) and older (24% aged 65 and over); about 250,000 more people left than arrived in 2011–2015.
Things that improved the whole time: people live longer (81.8 years, from 77.9 in 2000), almost everyone is online (86%, from 9%), and coal fell from 64% of the electricity to 5%.
Poverty here is the World Bank’s societal poverty line, which moves with what is normal in each country: the share of people living well below the usual Greek standard of living. It rose during the crisis and has since come back down.

title: What Greece Makes, Sells and Buys, and Can It Feed Itself?
text:
What does the Greek economy live on? This story follows the money through the economy and across its borders, and the food through its farms, seas and ports:

What does Greece produce?
Who buys it?
How much does Greece sell abroad, and how much does it buy?
What does it sell and buy, and with whom?
Can Greece feed itself?

The data come from three places:

Eurostat, the statistical office of the EU: the national accounts, which split the economy into what each industry produces and into who spends the money, and the balance of payments, which records what Greece sells and buys abroad in services, such as tourism and shipping.
Comext, Eurostat’s database of trade in goods, which records every good that crosses the borders of an EU country: what it is, where it comes from or goes to, and what it is worth.
FAOSTAT, the statistics of the Food and Agriculture Organization of the UN, whose food balance sheets weigh, for each food, what a country produces, imports, exports and eats.

They are downloaded when the document is knitted, so the charts show the latest figures.
