title: What Greece Makes, Sells and Buys, and Can It Feed Itself?
text:
Packages


Code
# install.packages(c("eurostat", "plotly", "jsonlite", "countrycode"))
library(eurostat)
library(plotly)

title: What Greece Makes, Sells and Buys, and Can It Feed Itself?
text:
The data


Code
# a Eurostat dataset, without its missing values, in the order of the years
eurostat_values <- function(id, filters) {
  x <- get_eurostat(id, filters = filters, time_format = "num", cache = FALSE)
  x <- as.data.frame(x[!is.na(x$values), ])
  x[order(x$time), ]
}

# the industries of the national accounts (NACE); energy, water and mining are all industry (B-E)
# without manufacturing (C)
industries <- c(
  A = "Agriculture, forestry and fishing", BE_C = "Energy, water and mining", C = "Manufacturing",
  F = "Construction", "G-I" = "Trade, transport, hotels and restaurants", J = "Information and communication",
  K = "Finance and insurance", L = "Real estate", M_N = "Professional and business services",
  "O-Q" = "Public administration, education and health", "R-U" = "Arts, leisure and other services"
)
# what each industry produces (gross value added, million euros) and the people who work in it (thousands)
gva <- eurostat_values("nama_10_a10", list(geo = c("EL", "EU27_2020"), unit = "CP_MEUR", na_item = "B1G"))
jobs <- eurostat_values("nama_10_a10_e", list(geo = c("EL", "EU27_2020"), unit = "THS_PER", na_item = "EMP_DC"))
# the share of each industry in the total, %
shares <- function(x, geo, year) {
  x <- x[x$geo == geo & x$time == year, ]
  v <- setNames(x$values, x$nace_r2)
  v["BE_C"] <- v["B-E"] - v["C"]
  100 * v[names(industries)] / v["TOTAL"]
}
gva_year <- max(gva$time[gva$geo == "EL"])
job_year <- max(jobs$time[jobs$geo == "EL"])

# GDP by who spends it, % of GDP and million euros: households (with the non-profit institutions that
# serve them), government, investment (gross capital formation), exports and imports, of goods and of services
uses <- c(P31_S14_S15 = "Households", P3_S13 = "Government", P5G = "Investment", P6 = "Exports", P7 = "Imports")
accounts <- eurostat_values("nama_10_gdp", list(
  geo = c("EL", "EU27_2020"), unit = c("PC_GDP", "CP_MEUR"), na_item = c(names(uses), "P61", "P62", "P71", "P72")
))
gdp_year <- max(accounts$time[accounts$geo == "EL"])
account <- function(item, geo = "EL", year = gdp_year, unit = "PC_GDP") {
  accounts$values[accounts$na_item == item & accounts$geo == geo & accounts$time == year & accounts$unit == unit]
}

# services sold to (CRE) and bought from (DEB) the rest of the world, million euros: all services (S),
# travel (SD), transport (SC), sea transport (SC1) and its freight (SC12)
services <- eurostat_values("bop_its6_det", list(
  geo = "EL", partner = "WRL_REST", currency = "MIO_EUR", stk_flow = c("CRE", "DEB"), bop_item = c("S", "SD", "SC", "SC1", "SC12")
))
service <- function(item, flow = "CRE", year) services$values[services$bop_item == item & services$stk_flow == flow & services$time == year]
services_year <- max(services$time[services$bop_item == "S"])
sea_year <- max(services$time[services$bop_item == "SC1"])

# Comext, Eurostat's database of trade in goods, from its own API (the eurostat package does not
# read it): a JSON-stat dataset, its values in one vector in the order of its dimensions, the last
# changing fastest
comext <- function(filters, id = "DS-045409") {
  query <- paste(paste0(rep(names(filters), lengths(filters)), "=", unlist(filters)), collapse = "&")
  x <- jsonlite::fromJSON(paste0("https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/api/comext/dissemination/statistics/1.0/data/", id, "?", query))
  codes <- lapply(x$id, function(d) names(sort(unlist(x$dimension[[d]]$category$index))))
  grid <- expand.grid(rev(codes), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)   # the first dimension changes fastest
  names(grid) <- rev(x$id)
  grid$values <- NA
  grid$values[as.integer(names(x$value)) + 1] <- unlist(x$value)
  grid <- grid[!is.na(grid$values), ]
  grid$time <- as.integer(grid$time)
  grid
}
# Greece's exports (flow 2) and imports (flow 1) of goods each year since 2019, in euros; with no
# partner, with each partner
trade <- function(product, partner = NULL) {
  comext(list(reporter = "GR", partner = partner, product = product, flow = c("1", "2"),
    indicators = "VALUE_IN_EUROS", freq = "A", sinceTimePeriod = "2019"))
}
# the chapters of the Harmonized System, the classification of goods in trade, by short names
chapters <- c(
  "01" = "Live animals", "02" = "Meat", "03" = "Fish and seafood", "04" = "Dairy, eggs and honey",
  "05" = "Other animal products", "06" = "Plants and flowers", "07" = "Vegetables", "08" = "Fruit and nuts",
  "09" = "Coffee, tea and spices", "10" = "Cereals", "11" = "Flour", "12" = "Oil seeds", "13" = "Gums and resins",
  "14" = "Other plant materials", "15" = "Olive oil and other fats", "16" = "Prepared meat and fish",
  "17" = "Sugar and sweets", "18" = "Cocoa and chocolate", "19" = "Bread, pasta and pastry",
  "20" = "Preserved fruit and vegetables", "21" = "Other food preparations", "22" = "Drinks",
  "23" = "Animal feed", "24" = "Tobacco", "25" = "Salt, stone and cement", "26" = "Ores",
  "27" = "Fuels and oil products", "28" = "Inorganic chemicals", "29" = "Organic chemicals", "30" = "Medicines",
  "31" = "Fertilisers", "32" = "Paints and dyes", "33" = "Cosmetics", "34" = "Soaps and detergents",
  "35" = "Glues and enzymes", "36" = "Explosives", "37" = "Photographic goods", "38" = "Other chemicals",
  "39" = "Plastics", "40" = "Rubber", "41" = "Hides and leather", "42" = "Leather goods", "43" = "Furs",
  "44" = "Wood", "45" = "Cork", "46" = "Basketwork", "47" = "Pulp", "48" = "Paper", "49" = "Printed matter",
  "50" = "Silk", "51" = "Wool", "52" = "Cotton", "53" = "Other plant fibres", "54" = "Man-made filaments",
  "55" = "Man-made fibres", "56" = "Wadding and ropes", "57" = "Carpets", "58" = "Special fabrics",
  "59" = "Coated fabrics", "60" = "Knitted fabrics", "61" = "Knitted clothes", "62" = "Other clothes",
  "63" = "Other textile articles", "64" = "Footwear", "65" = "Headwear", "66" = "Umbrellas",
  "67" = "Feathers and artificial flowers", "68" = "Stone articles", "69" = "Ceramics", "70" = "Glass",
  "71" = "Jewellery and gold", "72" = "Iron and steel", "73" = "Iron and steel articles", "74" = "Copper",
  "75" = "Nickel", "76" = "Aluminium", "78" = "Lead", "79" = "Zinc", "80" = "Tin", "81" = "Other base metals",
  "82" = "Tools", "83" = "Other metal articles", "84" = "Machinery", "85" = "Electrical equipment",
  "86" = "Railway equipment", "87" = "Cars and other vehicles", "88" = "Aircraft", "89" = "Ships and boats",
  "90" = "Instruments", "91" = "Clocks and watches", "92" = "Musical instruments", "93" = "Arms",
  "94" = "Furniture", "95" = "Toys and sports goods", "96" = "Other manufactured articles",
  "97" = "Art and antiques", "99" = "Other goods"
)
goods <- trade(names(chapters), "WORLD")
trade_year <- max(goods$time)
# exports and imports of each chapter in a year, million euros
by_chapter <- function(codes, year = trade_year) {
  x <- data.frame(code = codes, name = unname(chapters[codes]))
  x$exports <- sapply(codes, function(k) sum(goods$values[goods$product == k & goods$flow == "2" & goods$time == year])) / 1e6
  x$imports <- sapply(codes, function(k) sum(goods$values[goods$product == k & goods$flow == "1" & goods$time == year])) / 1e6
  x
}
# crude oil (2709), oil products (2710) and gas (2711)
oil <- trade(c("2709", "2710", "2711"), "WORLD")
oil_trade <- function(code, flow, year = trade_year) sum(oil$values[oil$product == code & oil$flow == flow & oil$time == year]) / 1e6
# the trading partners: countries only, with their names (Comext calls Serbia XS)
partners <- trade("TOTAL")
partners <- partners[partners$time == trade_year, ]
partners$name <- countrycode::countrycode(partners$partner, "iso2c", "country.name", warn = FALSE,
  custom_match = c(TR = "Türkiye", XS = "Serbia", XK = "Kosovo"))
partners <- partners[!is.na(partners$name), ]

# FAOSTAT's food balance sheets for the countries of Europe, from its bulk download, Greece only;
# quantities in thousand tonnes, and the calories of the food each person eats a day
fao_zip <- tempfile(fileext = ".zip")
download.file("https://bulks-faostat.fao.org/production/FoodBalanceSheets_E_Europe.zip", fao_zip, quiet = TRUE, mode = "wb")
fbs <- read.csv(unz(fao_zip, "FoodBalanceSheets_E_Europe_NOFLAG.csv"), check.names = FALSE)
fbs <- fbs[fbs$Area == "Greece", ]
fao_years <- as.integer(sub("^Y", "", grep("^Y[0-9]{4}$", names(fbs), value = TRUE)))
fao_year <- max(fao_years[sapply(fao_years, function(y) any(!is.na(fbs[fbs$Element == "Production", paste0("Y", y)])))])
balance <- function(code, element, year = fao_year) {
  v <- fbs[fbs$`Item Code` == code & fbs$Element == element, paste0("Y", year)]
  if (length(v) && !is.na(v[1])) v[1] else NA
}
# what Greece produces of a food, % of what it uses (production / domestic supply): its self-sufficiency
self_sufficiency <- function(code, year = fao_year) {
  produced <- balance(code, "Production", year)
  100 * (if (is.na(produced)) 0 else produced) / balance(code, "Domestic supply quantity", year)
}

eu_name <- c(EL = "Greece", EU27_2020 = "EU-27")




Code
greek_red <- "#d62728"
blue <- "#1f77b4"
gray <- "#9e9e9e"
dark_gray <- "#6b6b6b"   # also the color of the notes and the labels
amber <- "#c97b1e"       # told apart from blue also with colour blindness

# the source of a chart, as a note under it, and the common layout
chart <- function(p, title, source, y_title = "", y_axis = list(), x_axis = list(), annotations = list(), margin = list(t = 70, b = 90), note_y = -0.16, ...) {
  note <- list(
    text = paste("Source:", source), xref = "paper", yref = "paper", x = 0, y = note_y,
    xanchor = "left", yanchor = "top", showarrow = FALSE, font = list(size = 11, color = dark_gray)
  )
  layout(p,
    # at the top, so that a legend of two or three rows fits under it in a larger top margin
    title = list(text = title, x = 0.02, xanchor = "left", y = 0.97, yanchor = "top"),
    yaxis = c(list(title = y_title), y_axis),
    xaxis = c(list(title = ""), x_axis),
    margin = margin,
    annotations = c(annotations, list(note)),
    ...
  ) %>% config(displaylogo = FALSE)
}
legend_top <- list(orientation = "h", x = 0, y = 1.02, yanchor = "bottom")
# horizontal bars of two series side by side for each label, the labels from the top in their order
paired_bars <- function(labels, first, second, names, colors, hover) {
  y <- factor(labels, levels = rev(labels))
  plot_ly() %>%
    # plotly draws the first series at the bottom of each pair, so the second goes in first
    add_trace(y = y, x = second, type = "bar", orientation = "h", name = names[2], marker = list(color = colors[2]),
      hovertemplate = paste0("%{y}: ", hover, "<extra>", names[2], "</extra>")) %>%
    add_trace(y = y, x = first, type = "bar", orientation = "h", name = names[1], marker = list(color = colors[1]),
      hovertemplate = paste0("%{y}: ", hover, "<extra>", names[1], "</extra>"))
}

# short labels of numbers
percent <- function(x, digits = 0) paste0(format(round(x, digits), nsmall = digits, trim = TRUE), "%")
billion <- function(x) paste0("€", format(round(x / 1000, 1), nsmall = 1, trim = TRUE), " billion")   # from million euros
one <- function(x) format(round(x, 1), nsmall = 1, trim = TRUE)
# a country's name in a sentence: "the United States"
in_text <- function(name) ifelse(name %in% c("United Kingdom", "United States", "Netherlands"), paste("the", name), name)
# "A", "A and B", "A, B and C"
and_list <- function(x) if (length(x) < 2) x else paste(paste(x[-length(x)], collapse = ", "), "and", x[length(x)])

title: What Greece Makes, Sells and Buys, and Can It Feed Itself?
text:
1. What does Greece produce?


Code
greece <- shares(gva, "EL", gva_year)
eu <- shares(gva, "EU27_2020", gva_year)
greek_jobs <- shares(jobs, "EL", job_year)
eu_jobs <- shares(jobs, "EU27_2020", job_year)
# the industries with a larger share in Greece than in the EU, the largest difference first
larger <- names(sort((greece - eu)[greece > eu], decreasing = TRUE))
smaller <- names(sort((greece - eu)[greece < eu]))


Mostly services, and above all the ones that serve tourists. Of everything the Greek economy produced in 2025, 26% came from trade, transport, hotels and restaurants, against 19% in the EU. The industries with a larger share in Greece than in the EU are, above all, trade, transport, hotels and restaurants (25.5% against 18.6%), real estate (15.2% against 10.9%) and agriculture, forestry and fishing (4.1% against 1.8%); those with a smaller share, above all, professional and business services (7.2% against 11.9%), manufacturing (11.2% against 15.8%) and construction (2.6% against 5.6%).


Code
order <- names(sort(greece, decreasing = TRUE))
paired_bars(industries[order], greece[order], eu[order], c("Greece", "EU-27"), c(greek_red, blue), "%{x:.1f}% of the economy") %>%
  chart(paste0("What each industry produces, ", gva_year, ", % of the economy"), "Eurostat, nama_10_a10 (gross value added)",
    barmode = "group", legend = c(legend_top, traceorder = "reversed"), margin = list(l = 290, t = 100, b = 90), note_y = -0.1)






Three things stand out:

Real estate is 15% of the Greek economy. Most of it is not buying and selling houses: the national accounts count the rent that the people who own their homes would pay if they rented them, and most Greeks own their homes.
Construction has never recovered from the crisis: 7.8% of the economy in 2007, 2.6% in 2025.
Agriculture produces 4.1% of the economy but employs 9.3% of the people who work, against 3.8% in the EU: many small farms, each producing little. Trade, transport, hotels and restaurants employ 37% of the people who work.

title: What Greece Makes, Sells and Buys, and Can It Feed Itself?
text:
2. Who buys it?


Code
use_shares <- data.frame(item = names(uses), name = uses)
use_shares$greece <- sapply(names(uses), account)
use_shares$eu <- sapply(names(uses), account, geo = "EU27_2020")


Households. GDP is also what is spent on what the economy produces: by households, by the government, on investment, and by foreigners, as exports; and as part of what is spent is produced abroad, imports are taken off. In Greece, households spend 69% of GDP, against 53% in the EU, while investment, in buildings, machines and software, is 17% of GDP, against 22%. Greece consumes a larger share of what it produces, and invests a smaller share, than the EU, and it buys more from abroad than it sells: imports of 44% of GDP, exports of 39%.


Code
x <- factor(use_shares$name, levels = use_shares$name)
plot_ly() %>%
  add_trace(x = x, y = use_shares$greece, type = "bar", name = "Greece", marker = list(color = greek_red),
    hovertemplate = "%{x}: %{y:.1f}% of GDP<extra>Greece</extra>") %>%
  add_trace(x = x, y = use_shares$eu, type = "bar", name = "EU-27", marker = list(color = blue),
    hovertemplate = "%{x}: %{y:.1f}% of GDP<extra>EU-27</extra>") %>%
  chart(paste0("Who spends the money: GDP by use, ", gdp_year, ", % of GDP"), "Eurostat, nama_10_gdp", "% of GDP",
  barmode = "group", legend = legend_top,
  annotations = list(list(x = "Imports", y = max(use_shares$greece[5], use_shares$eu[5]), text = "taken off", yanchor = "bottom",
    yshift = 4, showarrow = FALSE, font = list(color = dark_gray))))

title: What Greece Makes, Sells and Buys, and Can It Feed Itself?
section: 3. How much does Greece sell abroad, and how much does it buy?
text:
3. How much does Greece sell abroad, and how much does it buy?


Code
exports <- accounts[accounts$geo == "EL" & accounts$na_item == "P6" & accounts$unit == "PC_GDP", c("time", "values")]
imports <- accounts[accounts$geo == "EL" & accounts$na_item == "P7" & accounts$unit == "PC_GDP", c("time", "values")]
first <- max(min(exports$time), 1995)
gap <- imports$values[match(exports$time, imports$time)] - exports$values   # % of GDP
surplus_years <- exports$time[exports$time >= first & gap < 0]
widest <- exports$time[exports$time >= first][which.max(gap[exports$time >= first])]
gap_in <- function(year) gap[exports$time == year]


Twice as open as in the 1990s. Greece’s exports of goods and services were 14% of GDP in 1995 and 39% in 2025; its imports, 22% and 44%. In every year since 1995 Greece has bought more from abroad than it sold. The gap was widest in 2008, 11.5 points of GDP, when Greece borrowed abroad to pay for its imports; in 2013, in the crisis, it was 2.3 points, as Greeks could afford much less.


Code
plot_ly(exports[exports$time >= first, ],
  x = ~time, y = ~values, type = "scatter", mode = "lines", name = "Exports",
  line = list(color = blue, width = 3), hovertemplate = "%{x}: %{y:.1f}% of GDP<extra>Exports</extra>"
) %>%
  add_trace(data = imports[imports$time >= first, ], x = ~time, y = ~values, name = "Imports",
    line = list(color = amber, width = 3), hovertemplate = "%{x}: %{y:.1f}% of GDP<extra>Imports</extra>",
    type = "scatter", mode = "lines", inherit = FALSE) %>%
  chart("Exports and imports of goods and services, % of GDP", "Eurostat, nama_10_gdp", "% of GDP",
    y_axis = list(rangemode = "tozero"), legend = legend_top)








Code
goods_gap <- account("P71", unit = "CP_MEUR") - account("P61", unit = "CP_MEUR")
services_gap <- account("P62", unit = "CP_MEUR") - account("P72", unit = "CP_MEUR")


Greece sells services and buys goods. In 2025, it bought €34.1 billion more goods abroad than it sold, and sold €22.5 billion more services than it bought. Two services earn almost all of it:

Tourism: in 2025, visitors from abroad spent €23.6 billion in Greece (see the story of Greek tourism).
Shipping: Greek shipowners have one of the largest merchant fleets of the world, and the freight their ships earn carrying goods between other countries counts as a Greek export. Sea transport brought in €18.3 billion in 2024, €16.9 billion of it freight.

Together, travel and transport were 83% of the services Greece sold in 2025.


Code
kinds <- c(Goods = "P61", Services = "P62")
bought <- c(Goods = "P71", Services = "P72")
plot_ly() %>%
  add_trace(x = names(kinds), y = sapply(kinds, account, unit = "CP_MEUR") / 1000, type = "bar", name = "Exports",
    marker = list(color = blue), hovertemplate = "%{x}: €%{y:.1f} billion<extra>Exports</extra>") %>%
  add_trace(x = names(bought), y = sapply(bought, account, unit = "CP_MEUR") / 1000, type = "bar", name = "Imports",
    marker = list(color = amber), hovertemplate = "%{x}: €%{y:.1f} billion<extra>Imports</extra>") %>%
  chart(paste0("Exports and imports of Greece, ", gdp_year, ", € billion"), "Eurostat, nama_10_gdp", "€ billion",
    barmode = "group", legend = legend_top)

title: What Greece Makes, Sells and Buys, and Can It Feed Itself?
section: 4. What does it sell and buy, and with whom?
text:
4. What does it sell and buy, and with whom?


Code
products <- by_chapter(names(chapters))
products$total <- products$exports + products$imports
top_products <- head(products[order(-products$total), ], 14)
top_exports <- head(products[order(-products$exports), ], 5)
fuel_share <- function(flow) 100 * products[[flow]][products$code == "27"] / sum(products[[flow]])


Oil, in both directions. In 2025, Greece exported €48.7 billion of goods and imported €82.5 billion. The largest exports were fuels and oil products (€12.7 billion), aluminium (€2.9 billion), medicines (€2.8 billion), electrical equipment (€2.4 billion) and machinery (€1.8 billion). Fuels are 26% of what Greece sells and 20% of what it buys, because its refineries import crude oil and export what they make of it: Greece bought €8.5 billion of crude oil and sold €10.4 billion of oil products, such as diesel, petrol and fuel for ships and aircraft. It also bought €3.3 billion of natural gas.
Of the rest, Greece imports far more machinery, electrical equipment and cars than it exports, and sells aluminium, medicines and food: fruit, preserved fruit and vegetables, cheese, fish and olive oil.


Code
paired_bars(top_products$name, top_products$exports / 1000, top_products$imports / 1000, c("Exports", "Imports"), c(blue, amber), "€%{x:.2f} billion") %>%
  chart(paste0("The goods Greece trades most, ", trade_year, ", € billion"), "Eurostat, Comext DS-045409 (chapters of the Harmonized System)",
    barmode = "group", legend = c(legend_top, traceorder = "reversed"), margin = list(l = 190, t = 100, b = 90), note_y = -0.12)








Code
by_partner <- data.frame(code = unique(partners$partner))
by_partner$name <- partners$name[match(by_partner$code, partners$partner)]
by_partner$exports <- sapply(by_partner$code, function(k) sum(partners$values[partners$partner == k & partners$flow == "2"])) / 1e6
by_partner$imports <- sapply(by_partner$code, function(k) sum(partners$values[partners$partner == k & partners$flow == "1"])) / 1e6
top_partners <- head(by_partner[order(-(by_partner$exports + by_partner$imports)), ], 12)
buyers <- head(by_partner[order(-by_partner$exports), ], 5)
sellers <- head(by_partner[order(-by_partner$imports), ], 5)
in_eu <- by_partner$code %in% eu_countries$code
eu_share <- function(flow) 100 * sum(by_partner[[flow]][in_eu]) / sum(by_partner[[flow]])
# countries outside the EU that sell Greece more than €1 billion a year and buy less than a quarter of that
one_way <- by_partner$name[!in_eu & by_partner$imports > 1000 & by_partner$exports < by_partner$imports / 4]


Mostly with its neighbours in the EU. 57% of the goods Greece sells go to the EU, and 55% of those it buys come from it. Its largest customers in 2025 were Italy, Germany, Cyprus, Bulgaria and the United States; its largest suppliers Germany, Italy, China, the Netherlands and France. Azerbaijan, China, India, Iraq, Kazakhstan and Russia sold Greece more than four times as much as they bought from it, mostly oil, gas or manufactured goods.


Code
paired_bars(top_partners$name, top_partners$exports / 1000, top_partners$imports / 1000, c("Exports to", "Imports from"), c(blue, amber), "€%{x:.2f} billion") %>%
  chart(paste0("Greece's largest trading partners in goods, ", trade_year, ", € billion"), "Eurostat, Comext DS-045409",
    barmode = "group", legend = c(legend_top, traceorder = "reversed"), margin = list(l = 150, t = 100, b = 90), note_y = -0.12)

title: What Greece Makes, Sells and Buys, and Can It Feed Itself?
text:
5. Can Greece feed itself?


Code
food <- by_chapter(names(chapters)[1:24])
food$balance <- food$exports - food$imports
food_then <- by_chapter(names(chapters)[1:24], 2019)


In money, Greece sells about as much food as it buys. In 2025, it exported €11.8 billion of food, drinks and tobacco and imported €12.7 billion, against €6.1 billion and €7.4 billion in 2019. But it sells and buys different foods. It sells more than it buys of preserved fruit and vegetables, fruit and nuts, olive oil and other fats, tobacco and fish and seafood; it buys far more than it sells of meat, animal feed, coffee, tea and spices, cocoa and chocolate and oil seeds. Meat alone costs it €1.8 billion more than it earns from it.


Code
shown <- food[abs(food$balance) >= 50, ]
shown <- shown[order(shown$balance), ]
plot_ly(
  y = factor(shown$name, levels = shown$name), x = shown$balance / 1000, type = "bar", orientation = "h",
  marker = list(color = ifelse(shown$balance > 0, blue, amber)),
  hovertext = paste0(shown$name, ": exports ", billion(shown$exports), ", imports ", billion(shown$imports)),
  hovertemplate = "%{hovertext}<extra></extra>"
) %>%
  chart(paste0("Food trade of Greece, exports minus imports, ", trade_year, ", € billion"),
    "Eurostat, Comext DS-045409 (chapters 1 to 24 of the Harmonized System; those under €50 million left out)",
    margin = list(l = 210, t = 70, b = 90), note_y = -0.1,
    annotations = list(
      # above the bars, on each side of zero
      list(x = 0, y = 1, yref = "paper", text = "Greece sells more →", xanchor = "left", yanchor = "bottom", xshift = 4, showarrow = FALSE, font = list(color = blue)),
      list(x = 0, y = 1, yref = "paper", text = "← Greece buys more", xanchor = "right", yanchor = "bottom", xshift = -4, showarrow = FALSE, font = list(color = amber))
    ))






Money does not tell how much of its food Greece grows. The food balance sheets of FAOSTAT do: for each food, they weigh what Greece produces against what it uses, for food, for animal feed and in factories. A food of which Greece produces more than 100% of what it uses is one it could do without importing; one far below 100% is one it depends on others for.


Code
foods <- c(
  "2580" = "Olive oil", "2919" = "Fruit", "2918" = "Vegetables", "2732" = "Lamb and goat", "2948" = "Milk",
  "2734" = "Poultry", "2949" = "Eggs", "2911" = "Pulses", "2511" = "Wheat", "2514" = "Maize", "2905" = "All cereals",
  "2943" = "All meat", "2907" = "Potatoes and other roots", "2960" = "Fish and seafood", "2733" = "Pork",
  "2731" = "Beef", "2909" = "Sugar and sweeteners", "2555" = "Soybeans"
)
fed <- data.frame(code = names(foods), name = foods)
fed$ratio <- sapply(fed$code, self_sufficiency)
ratio <- function(code) fed$ratio[fed$code == code]

# the calories of the diet, by the groups that together make up all of it, and the part of each that
# Greek production could cover if all of it stayed in Greece (up to what Greeks eat of it)
diet <- c("2905", "2907", "2908", "2909", "2911", "2912", "2913", "2914", "2918", "2919", "2922", "2923", "2924",
          "2943", "2945", "2946", "2948", "2949", "2960", "2961", "2928")
calories <- data.frame(code = diet, kcal = sapply(diet, balance, element = "Food supply (kcal/capita/day)"))
calories$ratio <- sapply(diet, self_sufficiency)
calories <- calories[!is.na(calories$kcal), ]
calories$covered <- calories$kcal * ifelse(is.na(calories$ratio), 0, pmin(calories$ratio, 100)) / 100
kcal_total <- sum(calories$kcal)
covered <- 100 * sum(calories$covered) / kcal_total
short <- calories$ratio < 70 | is.na(calories$ratio)


Plenty of olive oil, fruit and vegetables; not enough bread, meat or sugar. In 2023, Greece produced 351% of the olive oil it used, 163% of its fruit, 118% of its vegetables and 100% of its lamb and goat meat. But it produced only 66% of its cereals, 54% of its meat (25% of its pork and 24% of its beef), 29% of its fish and seafood and 10% of its sugar. It grows no soybeans, the protein of the feed of pigs and chickens.


Code
fed <- fed[order(fed$ratio), ]
plot_ly(
  y = factor(fed$name, levels = fed$name), x = fed$ratio, type = "bar", orientation = "h",
  marker = list(color = ifelse(fed$ratio >= 100, blue, amber)),
  hovertemplate = "%{y}: Greece produces %{x:.0f}% of what it uses<extra></extra>"
) %>%
  chart(paste0("What Greece produces, % of what it uses, ", fao_year), "FAOSTAT, food balance sheets (production / domestic supply)",
    margin = list(l = 180, t = 70, b = 90), note_y = -0.12,
    shapes = list(list(type = "line", x0 = 100, x1 = 100, y0 = 0, y1 = 1, yref = "paper", line = list(color = dark_gray, dash = "dash"))),
    # at the bottom, next to the shortest bars
    annotations = list(list(x = 100, y = 0, yref = "paper", text = "100%: as much as it uses", xanchor = "left", yanchor = "bottom",
      xshift = 4, showarrow = FALSE, font = list(color = dark_gray))))






Milk is the least certain of these figures. FAOSTAT counts cheese and yoghurt by the milk it takes to make them, and as Greece’s sales of feta and yoghurt abroad have grown, its milk has risen, on paper, from 56% of what it uses in 2010 to 121% in 2023, while its farms produced 97% of the milk they produced in 2010.
So, would Greece go hungry without imports? No, but it would eat differently. Greece has about 3,380 calories of food a day for each person who lives there: food available, not all of it eaten. If all the food that Greece produces stayed in Greece, it could cover about 70% of these calories, more than enough olive oil, fruit and vegetables but too little bread, pasta, meat and sugar: the foods of which Greece produces less than 70% of what it uses give 55% of the calories. And the figure flatters Greece, as its pigs and chickens eat feed made of imported soybeans and maize. For a country that sells olive oil, fruit and feta and buys meat, cereals and feed, what matters is to sell enough food to pay for the food it lacks, and in 2025 Greece’s food exports were worth 93% of its food imports.

title: What Greece Makes, Sells and Buys, and Can It Feed Itself?
text:
So, what does it mean?
The Greek economy is one of services, consumption and imports.

Services: trade, transport, hotels and restaurants make 26% of the economy, against 19% in the EU; manufacturing 11%, against 16%.
Consumption: households spend 69% of GDP, the EU’s 53%; investment is 17%, the EU’s 22%.
Trade: Greece sells tourism and shipping, and buys goods: €22.5 billion more services sold than bought, €34.1 billion more goods bought than sold in 2025. Its largest trade in goods is oil, bought crude and sold refined.
Food: about as much sold as bought, in money. Greece produces far more olive oil, fruit and vegetables than it eats, and depends on imports for cereals, meat, fish, sugar and animal feed.

title: What Greece Makes, Sells and Buys, and Can It Feed Itself?
text:
Sources

Eurostat: nama_10_a10 (gross value added by industry), nama_10_a10_e (employment by industry), nama_10_gdp (GDP and its uses), bop_its6_det (international trade in services).
Eurostat, Comext: DS-045409 (EU trade since 1988 by HS2-4-6 and CN8), through its API.
FAOSTAT: Food Balances (2010 onwards).

title: Greece’s Summer Economy: Who Comes, When, Where and What They Spend
text:
Greece is one of the most visited countries of Europe, and its tourism is squeezed into a few summer months and a few groups of islands. This story follows the tourists through the statistics of Eurostat:

How many come?
When do they come?
Where do they go?
Where do they come from?
How much do they spend, against other holiday countries?
How much does Greece depend on them?
Where do they stay?

The data come from three places, all at Eurostat, the statistical office of the EU:

The statistics of tourist accommodation: the nights that guests spend in hotels, rented rooms and apartments, and campsites, each month since 1994, by region and by the country the guests live in. A night is one guest staying one night: a couple on a week’s holiday spend 14 nights. Since 2018 Eurostat also counts the nights booked through Airbnb, Booking, Expedia and Tripadvisor.
The survey of the trips of EU residents, which asks people in every EU country where they travelled and what they spent. It tells what a holiday in Greece costs its visitors, against a holiday in Spain, Italy or Croatia.
The balance of payments, which records what foreign visitors spend in each country, so it can be set against the size of its economy.

They are downloaded when the document is knitted, so the charts show the latest figures.

title: Greece’s Summer Economy: Who Comes, When, Where and What They Spend

Greece is one of the most visited countries of Europe, and its tourism is squeezed into a few summer months and a few groups of islands. This story follows the tourists through the statistics of Eurostat:

How many come?

title: Greece’s Summer Economy: Who Comes, When, Where and What They Spend
text:
Packages


Code
# install.packages(c("eurostat", "plotly"))
library(eurostat)
library(plotly)

title: Greece’s Summer Economy: Who Comes, When, Where and What They Spend
text:
The data


Code
# a Eurostat dataset, without its missing values, in the order of the years
eurostat_values <- function(id, filters) {
  x <- get_eurostat(id, filters = filters, time_format = "num", cache = FALSE)
  x <- as.data.frame(x[!is.na(x$values), ])
  x[order(x$time), ]
}
# a monthly Eurostat dataset, the same way, with the year and the month of each value
eurostat_months <- function(id, filters) {
  x <- get_eurostat(id, filters = filters, time_format = "date", cache = FALSE)
  x <- as.data.frame(x[!is.na(x$values), ])
  x$year <- as.integer(format(x$time, "%Y"))
  x$month <- as.integer(format(x$time, "%m"))
  x[order(x$time), ]
}
eu <- eu_countries$code
eu_name <- c(setNames(eu_countries$name, eu_countries$code), EU27_2020 = "EU-27", TR = "Türkiye")

# Greece every year: the nights at all tourist accommodation (I551-I553), in hotels (I551), in rented
# rooms, apartments and holiday homes (I552, counted from 2009) and in campsites (I553), of all
# guests, of guests from abroad and of Greeks
kinds <- c(I551 = "Hotels", I552 = "Rented rooms and apartments", I553 = "Campsites")
annual <- eurostat_values("tour_occ_ninat", list(
  geo = "EL", unit = "NR", c_resid = c("TOTAL", "FOR", "DOM"), nace_r2 = c("I551-I553", names(kinds))
))
nights <- function(year, kind = "I551-I553", resid = "TOTAL") {
  annual$values[annual$time == year & annual$nace_r2 == kind & annual$c_resid == resid]
}
years <- annual$time[annual$nace_r2 == "I551-I553" & annual$c_resid == "TOTAL"]
year_now <- max(years)

# the nights of each month at all tourist accommodation, every EU country
monthly <- eurostat_months("tour_occ_nim", list(geo = c(eu, "EU27_2020"), unit = "NR", c_resid = "TOTAL", nace_r2 = "I551-I553"))
greece <- monthly[monthly$geo == "EL", ]
month_now <- max(greece$time)   # the latest month
full_year <- max(as.integer(names(which(table(greece$year) == 12))))   # the latest year with all twelve months

# the regions of Greece (NUTS 2): the nights of each month since 2020, also per thousand inhabitants,
# of all guests and of guests from abroad
regions <- c(
  EL30 = "Attica", EL41 = "North Aegean", EL42 = "South Aegean", EL43 = "Crete",
  EL51 = "Eastern Macedonia and Thrace", EL52 = "Central Macedonia", EL53 = "Western Macedonia",
  EL54 = "Epirus", EL61 = "Thessaly", EL62 = "Ionian Islands", EL63 = "Western Greece",
  EL64 = "Central Greece", EL65 = "Peloponnese"
)
regional <- eurostat_values("tour_occ_nin2m", list(geo = names(regions), unit = c("NR", "P_THAB"), c_resid = c("TOTAL", "FOR"), nace_r2 = "I551-I553"))
region_year <- max(regional$time)

# the nights in Greece by the country the guests live in; countries only, not groups such as EUR
origins <- eurostat_values("tour_occ_ninraw", list(geo = "EL", unit = "NR", nace_r2 = "I551-I553"))
origins <- origins[nchar(origins$c_resid) == 2, ]
origin_nights <- function(country, year) origins$values[match(paste(country, year), paste(origins$c_resid, origins$time))]

# the survey of trips: what EU residents spend on holidays (trips for personal purposes of one night or
# more) in each country, by kind of spending, and the number of those trips and of their nights
destinations <- c("EL", "ES", "IT", "PT", "HR", "CY", "MT", "FR", "AT", "BG", "TR")
parts <- c(TRA = "Getting there and around", ACCOM = "Accommodation", OTHER = "Food, drinks and everything else")
survey <- list(geo = c("EU27_2020", setdiff(destinations, "TR")), c_dest = c(destinations, "DOM"), purpose = "PER", duration = "N_GE1")
# all spending (TOTXDUR, without durable goods), on transport and on accommodation; the rest is
# "everything else", as some countries count cafés and restaurants apart and others do not
per_trip <- eurostat_values("tour_dem_extotw", c(survey, list(statinfo = "AVG_TRP", expend = c("TOTXDUR", "TRA", "ACCOM"))))
trips <- eurostat_values("tour_dem_ttw", survey)
trip_nights <- eurostat_values("tour_dem_tnw", survey)
# Eurostat gives the totals of each kind of spending only for the trips at home; for the others they
# are the spending per trip times the trips
spent <- merge(per_trip[c("geo", "c_dest", "time", "expend", "values")], trips[c("geo", "c_dest", "time", "values")],
  by = c("geo", "c_dest", "time"), suffixes = c("_per_trip", "_trips"))
spent$values <- spent$values_per_trip * spent$values_trips

# consumer prices, 2015 = 100, in Greece and in the EU
prices <- eurostat_values("prc_hicp_aind", list(geo = c("EL", "EU27_2020"), coicop = "CP00", unit = "INX_A_AVG"))

# what foreign visitors spend in each country (travel, in the balance of payments) and GDP, million euros
receipts <- eurostat_values("bop_its6_det", list(geo = c(eu, "TR"), bop_item = "SD", stk_flow = "CRE", partner = "WRL_REST", currency = "MIO_EUR"))
gdp <- eurostat_values("nama_10_gdp", list(geo = c(eu, "TR"), na_item = "B1GQ", unit = "CP_MEUR"))

# the nights booked through Airbnb, Booking, Expedia and Tripadvisor, Greece and its regions
platforms <- eurostat_values("tour_ce_omn12", list(geo = c("EL", names(regions)), indic_to = "NGT_SP", c_resid = "TOTAL", month = "TOTAL"))
platform_year <- max(platforms$time)
on_platforms <- function(geo, year = platform_year) platforms$values[platforms$geo == geo & platforms$time == year]




Code
greek_red <- "#d62728"
blue <- "#1f77b4"
gray <- "#9e9e9e"
dark_gray <- "#6b6b6b"   # also the color of the notes and the labels
amber <- "#c97b1e"
# the three parts of a stacked bar, told apart also with colour blindness: light blue, amber, dark blue
stack_colors <- c("#5b8fd6", amber, "#1c5cab")
# a scale from few nights (white) to many (dark blue)
blues <- list(c(0, "#f4f8fd"), c(0.5, "#3987e5"), c(1, "#0d366b"))

# the source of a chart, as a note under it, and the common layout
chart <- function(p, title, source, y_title = "", y_axis = list(), x_axis = list(), annotations = list(), margin = list(t = 70, b = 90), note_y = -0.16, ...) {
  note <- list(
    text = paste("Source:", source), xref = "paper", yref = "paper", x = 0, y = note_y,
    xanchor = "left", yanchor = "top", showarrow = FALSE, font = list(size = 11, color = dark_gray)
  )
  layout(p,
    # at the top, so that a legend of two or three rows fits under it in a larger top margin
    title = list(text = title, x = 0.02, xanchor = "left", y = 0.97, yanchor = "top"),
    yaxis = c(list(title = y_title), y_axis),
    xaxis = c(list(title = ""), x_axis),
    margin = margin,
    annotations = c(annotations, list(note)),
    ...
  ) %>% config(displaylogo = FALSE)
}
legend_top <- list(orientation = "h", x = 0, y = 1.02, yanchor = "bottom")
months <- factor(month.abb, levels = month.abb)   # in this order on an axis
# a horizontal bar chart of countries or regions, from the highest at the top: by default one of
# them in red, the EU in blue and the others in gray
ranking_bars <- function(x, value, highlight, hover,
                         colors = function(x) ifelse(x$geo == highlight, greek_red, ifelse(x$geo == "EU27_2020", blue, gray))) {
  x <- x[order(x[[value]]), ]
  plot_ly(
    y = factor(x$name, levels = x$name), x = x[[value]], type = "bar", orientation = "h",
    marker = list(color = colors(x)), hovertext = hover(x), hovertemplate = "%{hovertext}<extra></extra>"
  )
}

# short labels of numbers
million <- function(x, digits = 1) paste(format(round(x / 1e6, digits), nsmall = digits, trim = TRUE), "million")
euros <- function(x) paste0("€", format(round(x), big.mark = ",", trim = TRUE))
billion_euros <- function(x) paste0("€", format(round(x / 1000, 1), nsmall = 1, trim = TRUE), " billion")   # from million euros
percent <- function(x, digits = 0) paste0(format(round(x, digits), nsmall = digits, trim = TRUE), "%")
one <- function(x) format(round(x, 1), nsmall = 1, trim = TRUE)
# "A", "A and B", "A, B and C"
and_list <- function(x) if (length(x) < 2) x else paste(paste(x[-length(x)], collapse = ", "), "and", x[length(x)])
# the place of a country counted from the highest: 1 is the highest
highest <- function(k) {
  if (k > 8) return(paste0("the ", k, "th highest"))
  paste0("the ", c("", "second ", "third ", "fourth ", "fifth ", "sixth ", "seventh ", "eighth ")[k], "highest")
}

title: Greece’s Summer Economy: Who Comes, When, Where and What They Spend
text:
1. How many come?


Code
record <- years[which.max(sapply(years, nights))]
foreign_share <- function(year) 100 * nights(year, resid = "FOR") / nights(year)
hotels_growth <- 100 * (nights(year_now, "I551") / nights(min(years), "I551") - 1)
covid_fall <- 100 * (1 - nights(2020) / nights(2019))
recovered <- min(years[years > 2020 & sapply(years, nights) > nights(2019)])
# this year so far, against the same months of last year
latest_year <- as.integer(format(month_now, "%Y"))
latest_month <- as.integer(format(month_now, "%m"))
so_far <- function(year) sum(greece$values[greece$year == year & greece$month <= latest_month])


156.3 million nights in 2025, more than ever.
In 2025, guests spent 156.3 million nights in the hotels, rented rooms and apartments, and campsites of Greece, 84% of them guests from abroad. Hotels alone had 119.0 million nights, 129% more than in 1994. In the first 8 months of 2026 there were 1.8% more nights than in the same months of 2025.
Until 2008 Greece counted only the nights in hotels and campsites; from 2009 it counts those in rented rooms, apartments and holiday homes too, so the bars jump in 2009. Since then the nights fell twice: in the debt crisis, to 80.6 million in 2012, and in 2020, when COVID closed the borders, by 73%. By 2023 there were more than in 2019.


Code
kind_colors <- c(I551 = stack_colors[3], I552 = stack_colors[2], I553 = stack_colors[1])
p <- plot_ly()
for (k in names(kinds)) {
  x <- annual[annual$nace_r2 == k & annual$c_resid == "TOTAL", ]
  p <- add_trace(p,
    x = x$time, y = x$values / 1e6, type = "bar", name = kinds[[k]],
    marker = list(color = kind_colors[[k]], line = list(color = "white", width = 1)),
    hovertemplate = paste0("%{x}: %{y:.1f} million nights<extra>", kinds[[k]], "</extra>")
  )
}
p %>% chart("Nights at tourist accommodation in Greece, million", "Eurostat, tour_occ_ninat", "Million",
  barmode = "stack", bargap = 0.15, legend = c(legend_top, traceorder = "normal"), margin = list(t = 100, b = 90),
  annotations = list(list(x = 2009, y = nights(2009) / 1e6, text = "2009: rented rooms and<br>apartments counted too",
    showarrow = TRUE, ax = -70, ay = -45, font = list(color = dark_gray))))






More and more of the guests come from abroad: 69% of the nights in 2010, 84% in 2025. In 2020, with few foreigners able to travel, the share fell to 68%.

title: Greece’s Summer Economy: Who Comes, When, Where and What They Spend
text:
2. When do they come?


Code
in_month <- function(year, month) greece$values[greece$year == year & greece$month == month]
in_months <- function(year, months) sum(greece$values[greece$year == year & greece$month %in% months])
summer <- 6:9
winter <- c(1:3, 11:12)
summer_share <- 100 * in_months(full_year, summer) / in_months(full_year, 1:12)
summer_growth <- in_months(full_year, summer) - in_months(2010, summer)
winter_growth <- in_months(full_year, winter) - in_months(2010, winter)


In August, 21 times as many nights as in January.
In 2025, guests spent 1.6 million nights in Greece in January and 34.0 million in August. 72% of the nights of the year fell in the four months from June to September. Each row of the chart is a year and each cell a month: the darker the cell, the more nights. Greece has added summer, not winter: from 2010 to 2025, the nights from June to September grew by 49.5 million, those from November to March by 4.2 million.


Code
heat <- greece[greece$year >= 2009, ]
z <- tapply(heat$values / 1e6, list(heat$year, factor(heat$month, levels = 1:12)), sum)   # years in rows, months in columns
plot_ly(
  x = months, y = rownames(z), z = z, type = "heatmap", colorscale = blues, xgap = 2, ygap = 2,
  colorbar = list(title = list(text = "Million<br>nights"), thickness = 12),
  hovertemplate = "%{x} %{y}: %{z:.1f} million nights<extra></extra>"
) %>%
  chart("Nights in Greece each month, million",
    paste0("Eurostat, tour_occ_nim, January 2009 to ", month.name[latest_month], " ", latest_year, "; blank: no data"), y_axis = list(type = "category", autorange = "reversed"), note_y = -0.08)








Code
season <- monthly[monthly$year == full_year, ]
complete <- names(which(table(season$geo) == 12))
by_season <- data.frame(geo = complete, name = eu_name[complete])
by_season$share <- sapply(complete, function(k) {
  x <- season[season$geo == k, ]
  100 * sum(x$values[x$month %in% summer]) / sum(x$values)
})
season_order <- by_season$geo[by_season$geo != "EU27_2020"][order(-by_season$share[by_season$geo != "EU27_2020"])]
more_seasonal <- season_order[seq_len(match("EL", season_order) - 1)]
eu_share <- by_season$share[by_season$geo == "EU27_2020"]


One of the most seasonal in the EU. In the EU as a whole, 52% of the nights at tourist accommodation fall from June to September; in Greece, 72%. Only Croatia packs more of its tourism into them. Hotels, restaurants and the people who work in them have to earn the year’s living in a few months.


Code
ranking_bars(by_season, "share", "EL", function(x) paste0(x$name, ": ", percent(x$share, 1), " of the year's nights")) %>%
  chart(paste0("Share of the nights of ", full_year, " spent from June to September, %"), "Eurostat, tour_occ_nim",
    margin = list(l = 130, t = 70, b = 90), note_y = -0.1)

title: Greece’s Summer Economy: Who Comes, When, Where and What They Spend
text:
3. Where do they go?


Code
year_total <- regional[regional$time == region_year & regional$month == "TOTAL", ]
region_value <- function(unit, resid) {
  year_total$values[match(paste(names(regions), unit, resid), paste(year_total$geo, year_total$unit, year_total$c_resid))]
}
by_region <- data.frame(geo = names(regions), name = regions)
by_region$nights <- region_value("NR", "TOTAL")
by_region$per_person <- region_value("P_THAB", "TOTAL") / 1000
by_region$foreign <- 100 * region_value("NR", "FOR") / by_region$nights
islands <- c("EL42", "EL43", "EL62")
islands_foreign <- min(by_region$foreign[by_region$geo %in% islands])
islands_share <- 100 * sum(by_region$nights[by_region$geo %in% islands]) / sum(by_region$nights)
in_region <- function(geo, column) by_region[[column]][by_region$geo == geo]
# the share of the nights of the year that a region has in each month
m <- regional[regional$time == region_year & regional$unit == "NR" & regional$c_resid == "TOTAL" & regional$month != "TOTAL", ]
m$month <- as.integer(sub("M", "", m$month))
by_month <- function(geo) {
  x <- m[m$geo == geo, ]
  x <- x[order(x$month), ]
  100 * x$values / sum(x$values)
}
summer_of <- function(geo) sum(by_month(geo)[summer])


62% of the nights on three groups of islands. In 2025, the South Aegean, the Cyclades and the Dodecanese with Santorini, Mykonos, Rhodes and Kos, had 41.8 million nights; Crete 35.2 million; the Ionian Islands, with Corfu, Zakynthos and Kefalonia, 20.4 million. Attica, with Athens, had 12.8 million. Against the people who live there, the islands are full: 128 nights a year for each inhabitant of the South Aegean and 103 in the Ionian Islands, against 3.4 in Attica. On the islands, 91% or more of the nights are those of guests from abroad.


Code
by_region$million_nights <- by_region$nights / 1e6
ranking_bars(by_region, "million_nights", "", function(x) {
  paste0(x$name, ": ", million(x$nights), " nights, ", round(x$per_person, 1), " per inhabitant, ", percent(x$foreign), " from abroad")
}, colors = function(x) ifelse(x$geo %in% islands, blue, gray)) %>%
  chart(paste0("Nights at tourist accommodation by region, ", region_year, ", million"), "Eurostat, tour_occ_nin2m",
    margin = list(l = 200, t = 70, b = 90))






Athens works all year, the islands in the summer. 80% of the nights of the Ionian Islands and 74% of those of the South Aegean fall from June to September, against 49% in Attica, where city breaks, business and conferences fill the hotels in spring and autumn too.


Code
shown <- c(EL62 = amber, EL42 = stack_colors[3], EL43 = stack_colors[1], EL30 = gray)
p <- plot_ly()
for (k in names(shown)) {
  p <- add_trace(p,
    x = months, y = by_month(k), type = "scatter", mode = "lines+markers", name = regions[[k]],
    line = list(color = shown[[k]], width = if (k == "EL30") 2 else 3, dash = if (k == "EL30") "dash" else "solid"),
    marker = list(color = shown[[k]], size = 8),
    hovertemplate = paste0("%{x}: %{y:.1f}% of the year<extra>", regions[[k]], "</extra>")
  )
}
p %>% chart(paste0("Share of the nights of ", region_year, " in each month, %"), "Eurostat, tour_occ_nin2m", "% of the year",
  y_axis = list(rangemode = "tozero"), legend = legend_top, margin = list(t = 100, b = 90))

title: Greece’s Summer Economy: Who Comes, When, Where and What They Spend
text:
4. Where do they come from?


Code
origin_year <- max(origins$time)
latest <- origins[origins$time == origin_year, ]
latest <- latest[order(-latest$values), ]
latest$name <- as.character(label_eurostat(latest$c_resid, dic = "c_resid"))
latest$name[latest$c_resid == "EL"] <- "Greece (Greeks at home)"
abroad <- latest[latest$c_resid != "EL", ]
# a country's name in a sentence: "the United Kingdom"
in_text <- function(name) ifelse(name %in% c("United Kingdom", "United States", "Netherlands"), paste("the", name), name)
share_of_foreign <- function(country) 100 * origin_nights(country, origin_year) / nights(origin_year, resid = "FOR")
change <- function(country, from = 2019) origin_nights(country, origin_year) - origin_nights(country, from)


Most come from the United Kingdom and Germany. In 2025, guests from the United Kingdom spent 25.4 million nights in Greece and those from Germany 21.0 million: together 35% of the nights of guests from abroad. Greeks on holiday in their own country spent 25.3 million.
The list has changed since 2019. The Russians, who spent 6.6 million nights in Greece in 2019, have almost gone since the EU closed its skies to Russian planes in 2022: 0.36 million in 2025. The Americans came in their place: 6.1 million nights, against 3.9 million in 2019. Poland and Romania grew too, by 1.3 million and 1.9 million nights.


Code
top <- head(latest, 12)
top <- top[order(top$values), ]
plot_ly(
  y = factor(top$name, levels = top$name), x = top$values / 1e6, type = "bar", orientation = "h",
  marker = list(color = ifelse(top$c_resid == "EL", gray, blue)),
  hovertext = paste0(top$name, ": ", million(top$values), " nights in ", origin_year, ", ",
    million(origin_nights(top$c_resid, 2019)), " in 2019"),
  hovertemplate = "%{hovertext}<extra></extra>"
) %>%
  chart(paste0("Nights in Greece by the country of the guests, ", origin_year, ", million"),
    "Eurostat, tour_occ_ninraw", margin = list(l = 190, t = 70, b = 90))

title: Greece’s Summer Economy: Who Comes, When, Where and What They Spend
section: 5. How much do they spend, against other holiday countries?
text:
5. How much do they spend, against other holiday countries?
Eurostat’s survey of trips asks people in every EU country where they went on holiday and what it cost them. The trips to a country include those of its own people on holiday at home, which are cheaper, as there is no long journey: so they are taken out here, and what remains are the visitors from the other EU countries. Türkiye, outside the EU, is in the comparison as Greece’s nearest competitor; all its visitors in the survey come from abroad.


Code
# the value for the visitors to a country from the other EU countries: all EU residents, minus its
# own residents on holiday at home (Türkiye has none in the survey)
from_abroad <- function(x, country, year) {
  everyone <- x$values[x$geo == "EU27_2020" & x$c_dest == country & x$time == year]
  at_home <- if (country == "TR") 0 else x$values[x$geo == country & x$c_dest == "DOM" & x$time == year]
  if (length(everyone) != 1 || length(at_home) != 1) return(NA)
  everyone - at_home
}
spending <- function(year) {
  x <- data.frame(geo = destinations, name = eu_name[destinations])
  for (p in c("TOTXDUR", "TRA", "ACCOM")) x[[p]] <- sapply(destinations, function(d) from_abroad(spent[spent$expend == p, ], d, year))
  x$OTHER <- x$TOTXDUR - x$TRA - x$ACCOM
  x$trips <- sapply(destinations, function(d) from_abroad(trips, d, year))
  x$nights <- sapply(destinations, function(d) from_abroad(trip_nights, d, year))
  x$per_trip <- x$TOTXDUR / x$trips
  x$per_night <- x$per_trip * x$trips / x$nights
  x$length <- x$nights / x$trips
  x[!is.na(x$per_trip), ]
}
survey_year <- max(trips$time[trips$geo == "EU27_2020" & trips$c_dest == "EL"])
costs <- spending(survey_year)
cost <- function(geo, column = "per_trip") costs[[column]][costs$geo == geo]
part_cost <- function(geo, part) cost(geo, part) / cost(geo, "trips")
by_trip <- costs$geo[order(-costs$per_trip)]
by_night <- costs$geo[order(-costs$per_night)]
by_length <- costs$geo[order(-costs$length)]
# the countries ahead of Greece in a ranking
before_greece <- function(ranking) ranking[seq_len(match("EL", ranking) - 1)]


A holiday in Greece costs its visitors €1,256, the third highest of the 11 holiday countries in the chart.
In 2025, visitors from the other EU countries spent €1,256 on a holiday trip to Greece, against €1,152 in Spain, €970 in Italy and €888 in Croatia; only Cyprus and Türkiye cost more. The money includes the journey: €379 of it went on getting there and around, mostly on the flights; €436 on accommodation; and €441 on food, drinks and everything else.


Code
costs <- costs[order(costs$per_trip), ]
labels <- ifelse(costs$geo == "EL", "<b>Greece</b>", costs$name)
y <- factor(labels, levels = labels)
p <- plot_ly()
for (k in seq_along(parts)) {
  p <- add_trace(p,
    y = y, x = costs[[names(parts)[k]]] / costs$trips, type = "bar", orientation = "h", name = parts[[k]],
    marker = list(color = stack_colors[k], line = list(color = "white", width = 1)),
    hovertemplate = paste0("%{y}: €%{x:,.0f}<extra>", parts[[k]], "</extra>")
  )
}
p %>% chart(paste0("What a holiday trip costs, ", survey_year, ", euros"),
  "Eurostat, tour_dem_extotw and tour_dem_ttw: visitors from the other EU countries; own calculation",
  x_axis = list(range = c(0, 1.15 * max(costs$per_trip))),
  barmode = "stack", legend = c(legend_top, traceorder = "normal"), margin = list(l = 110, t = 100, b = 90),
  annotations = lapply(seq_len(nrow(costs)), function(k) {
    list(x = costs$per_trip[k], y = labels[k], text = euros(costs$per_trip[k]), xanchor = "left", xshift = 4,
      showarrow = FALSE, font = list(color = dark_gray))
  }))






Per night, too, Greece is among the dearest. Visitors stay long in Greece, 8.6 nights a trip (only in Türkiye and Spain do they stay longer), so the cost of the flight is spread over more nights. A night of holiday in Greece costs them €145, the third highest of the 11: Cyprus (€173) and Malta (€163) cost more.


Code
ranking_bars(costs, "per_night", "EL", function(x) {
  paste0(x$name, ": ", euros(x$per_night), " a night, ", one(x$length), " nights a trip")
}) %>%
  chart(paste0("What a night of holiday costs, ", survey_year, ", euros"),
    "Eurostat, tour_dem_extotw and tour_dem_tnw: visitors from the other EU countries; own calculation",
    margin = list(l = 110, t = 70, b = 90))








Code
trip_cost <- function(year) {
  x <- spending(year)
  x$per_trip[x$geo == "EL"]
}
price_year <- min(survey_year, max(prices$time))
price_change <- function(geo) 100 * (prices$values[prices$geo == geo & prices$time == price_year] / prices$values[prices$geo == geo & prices$time == 2019] - 1)
cost_change <- 100 * (trip_cost(survey_year) / trip_cost(2019) - 1)
real_change <- c(100 * ((1 + cost_change / 100) / (1 + price_change("EL") / 100) - 1),
                 100 * ((1 + cost_change / 100) / (1 + price_change("EU27_2020") / 100) - 1))
# within 5% of 2019 after inflation, by the prices of Greece and of the EU, is "about the same"
real_spending <- if (all(abs(real_change) < 5)) "about the same" else if (all(real_change > 0)) "more" else if (all(real_change < 0)) "less" else "about the same"


More visitors, not richer ones. In 2019, a holiday trip to Greece cost visitors from the other EU countries €1,025; in 2025, €1,256, 23% more. Consumer prices rose by 20% in Greece and by 26% in the EU over the same years, so after inflation each visitor spends about what they spent in 2019: what has grown is the number of visitors. The survey asks a sample of people, so the figure of a single year can jump: it is the change over several years that counts.

title: Greece’s Summer Economy: Who Comes, When, Where and What They Spend
section: 6. How much does Greece depend on them?
text:
6. How much does Greece depend on them?


Code
both <- merge(receipts[c("geo", "time", "values")], gdp[c("geo", "time", "values")], by = c("geo", "time"), suffixes = c("_receipts", "_gdp"))
both$share <- 100 * both$values_receipts / both$values_gdp
receipts_year <- max(both$time[both$geo == "EL"])
share_of <- function(geo, year = receipts_year) both$share[both$geo == geo & both$time == year]
earned <- function(geo, year = receipts_year) both$values_receipts[both$geo == geo & both$time == year]
dependence <- both[both$time == receipts_year, ]
dependence$name <- eu_name[dependence$geo]
by_share <- dependence$geo[order(-dependence$share)]
ahead_of_greece <- by_share[seq_len(match("EL", by_share) - 1)]


€23.6 billion in 2025, 9.5% of GDP. That is what visitors from abroad spent in Greece, on hotels, meals, transport and shopping, without the flights to get there. Of the countries in the chart, only Croatia (16.3%), Malta (12.1%) and Cyprus (10.9%) depend more on them; in Spain they spent 6.2% of GDP, in Italy 2.5%. The figure counts only what foreigners spend: the holidays of Greeks at home, and the farms, builders and shops that sell to hotels, add to what the economy owes to tourism.


Code
ranking_bars(dependence, "share", "EL", function(x) paste0(x$name, ": ", percent(x$share, 1), " of GDP, ", billion_euros(x$values_receipts))) %>%
  chart(paste0("What visitors from abroad spend, ", receipts_year, ", % of GDP"),
    "Eurostat, bop_its6_det (travel, credit) and nama_10_gdp", margin = list(l = 130, t = 70, b = 90), note_y = -0.1)






What a country depends on, it can lose. In 2020 visitors from abroad spent €4.3 billion in Greece, 2.6% of GDP, against €18.2 billion in 2019.


Code
greek <- both[both$geo == "EL", ]
plot_ly(greek,
  x = ~time, y = ~share, type = "scatter", mode = "lines+markers", name = "Greece",
  line = list(color = greek_red, width = 3), marker = list(color = greek_red, size = 8),
  hovertext = paste0(greek$time, ": ", percent(greek$share, 1), " of GDP, ", billion_euros(greek$values_receipts)),
  hovertemplate = "%{hovertext}<extra></extra>"
) %>%
  chart("What visitors from abroad spend in Greece, % of GDP", "Eurostat, bop_its6_det (travel, credit) and nama_10_gdp",
    "% of GDP", y_axis = list(rangemode = "tozero"))

title: Greece’s Summer Economy: Who Comes, When, Where and What They Spend
text:
7. Where do they stay?


Code
compare_year <- min(platform_year, year_now)
platform_growth <- 100 * (on_platforms("EL", compare_year) / on_platforms("EL", 2019) - 1)
registered_growth <- 100 * (nights(compare_year) / nights(2019) - 1)
platforms_grew_more <- on_platforms("EL", compare_year) - on_platforms("EL", 2019) > nights(compare_year) - nights(2019)
stay_year <- min(platform_year, region_year)
stays <- regional[regional$time == stay_year & regional$month == "TOTAL" & regional$unit == "NR" & regional$c_resid == "TOTAL", ]
by_region$registered <- stays$values[match(by_region$geo, stays$geo)]
by_region$platforms <- sapply(by_region$geo, on_platforms, year = stay_year)
by_region$per_100 <- 100 * by_region$platforms / by_region$registered
platforms_per_100 <- function(geo) by_region$per_100[by_region$geo == geo]
more_than_attica <- by_region$name[by_region$per_100 > platforms_per_100("EL30")]


More and more of them in flats let through Airbnb and the like. In 2025, guests spent 52.1 million nights in places booked through Airbnb, Booking, Expedia or Tripadvisor, 115% more than in 2019. The nights in hotels, rented rooms and campsites grew by 9% in the same years. Some places are listed on the platforms and also counted as tourist accommodation, so the two cannot simply be added; but the platforms gained 27.8 million nights since 2019, the tourist accommodation 12.8 million: most of the growth has gone to the platforms.


Code
since <- min(platforms$time)
registered <- data.frame(time = since:year_now)
registered$values <- sapply(registered$time, nights)
greek_platforms <- platforms[platforms$geo == "EL", ]
plot_ly(registered,
  x = ~time, y = ~ values / 1e6, type = "scatter", mode = "lines+markers", name = "Hotels, rented rooms and campsites",
  line = list(color = blue, width = 3), marker = list(color = blue, size = 8),
  hovertemplate = "%{x}: %{y:.1f} million nights<extra>Tourist accommodation</extra>"
) %>%
  add_trace(data = greek_platforms, x = ~time, y = ~ values / 1e6, name = "Booked through the platforms",
    line = list(color = amber, width = 3), marker = list(color = amber, size = 8),
    hovertemplate = "%{x}: %{y:.1f} million nights<extra>Platforms</extra>", inherit = FALSE,
    type = "scatter", mode = "lines+markers") %>%
  chart("Nights in Greece, million", "Eurostat, tour_occ_ninat and tour_ce_omn12 (Airbnb, Booking, Expedia, Tripadvisor)",
    "Million", y_axis = list(rangemode = "tozero"), legend = legend_top)






In Athens, 81 nights on the platforms for every 100 in tourist accommodation. That is what Attica had in 2025, more than any other region; the South Aegean had 22 and Crete 25. Many of the flats let to visitors in Athens were once let to people who live there, which is one reason given for the rise of rents in the city; the story of Greek housing follows rents and house prices against incomes.


Code
x <- by_region[order(by_region$registered), ]
y <- factor(x$name, levels = x$name)
plot_ly(
  y = y, x = x$registered / 1e6, type = "bar", orientation = "h", name = "Hotels, rented rooms and campsites",
  marker = list(color = blue), hovertemplate = "%{y}: %{x:.1f} million nights<extra>Tourist accommodation</extra>"
) %>%
  add_trace(y = y, x = x$platforms / 1e6, name = "Booked through the platforms", marker = list(color = amber),
    hovertemplate = "%{y}: %{x:.1f} million nights<extra>Platforms</extra>") %>%
  chart(paste0("Nights by region, ", stay_year, ", million"), "Eurostat, tour_occ_nin2m and tour_ce_omn12",
    barmode = "group", legend = legend_top, margin = list(l = 200, t = 100, b = 90), note_y = -0.12)

title: Greece’s Summer Economy: Who Comes, When, Where and What They Spend
text:
So, what does it mean?
Tourism is one of the pillars of the Greek economy, and one of its risks. Visitors from abroad spend 9.5% of GDP in Greece, and they spend it:

In the summer: 72% of the nights fall from June to September. Greece has grown its summers, not its winters, so jobs and incomes in tourism remain seasonal.
On the islands: 62% of the nights are spent in the South Aegean, Crete and the Ionian Islands, where there are 128 nights for each inhabitant of the South Aegean every year, with what that means for water, roads and housing in August.
On long trips: a holiday in Greece costs its visitors from the rest of the EU €1,256, the third highest of the 11 holiday countries in the chart, and a night €145, the third highest. After inflation, each visitor spends about as much as before COVID: the growth comes from more visitors.
Through the platforms: since 2019, nights booked through Airbnb and the like grew by 115%, the registered tourist accommodation by 9%.

2020 showed the risk: when the visitors could not come, 73% of the nights were lost in one year. Longer seasons, more regions and more visitors from outside Europe would spread it.

title: Greece’s Summer Economy: Who Comes, When, Where and What They Spend
text:
Sources

Eurostat, tourist accommodation: tour_occ_ninat (nights per year), tour_occ_nim (nights per month), tour_occ_nin2m (nights by month and region), tour_occ_ninraw (nights by the country of the guests), tour_ce_omn12 (short-stay accommodation booked through online platforms).
Eurostat, trips of EU residents: tour_dem_extotw (expenditure per trip by destination), tour_dem_ttw (trips by destination), tour_dem_tnw (nights by destination).
Eurostat, economy: bop_its6_det (international trade in services: travel), nama_10_gdp (GDP), prc_hicp_aind (consumer prices).

title: Arctic Sea Ice Is Melting
text:
Every September the Arctic sea ice reaches its annual minimum after the summer melt season. The National Snow and Ice Data Center (NSIDC) has been tracking this since 1979 using satellite passive-microwave sensors. Their Sea Ice Index v4.0 is the authoritative public record.
This document shows you exactly how to download the real data and reproduce the charts below — no manual downloads, no hardcoded numbers.

title: Arctic Sea Ice Is Melting
text:
Every September the Arctic sea ice reaches its annual minimum after the summer melt season. The National Snow and Ice Data Center (NSIDC) has been tracking this since 1979 using satellite passive-microwave sensors. Their Sea Ice Index v4.0 is the authoritative public record.
This document shows you exactly how to download the real data and reproduce the charts below — no manual downloads, no hardcoded numbers.

title: Arctic Sea Ice Is Melting
text:
Packages


Code
# Install any missing packages before running
# install.packages(c("ggplot2", "dplyr", "sf", "rnaturalearth", "rnaturalearthdata"))

library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(sf)
library(rnaturalearth)

title: Arctic Sea Ice Is Melting
text:
Part 1 — Time series

Download the data
NSIDC publishes one CSV per month. September (month 09) is the annual minimum.


Code
csv_url <- "https://noaadata.apps.nsidc.org/NOAA/G02135/north/monthly/data/N_09_extent_v4.0.csv"

arctic <- read.csv(csv_url, strip.white = TRUE) |>
  select(year, extent) |>
  filter(year >= 1979)

head(arctic)


  year extent
1 1979   7.05
2 1980   7.67
3 1981   7.14
4 1982   7.30
5 1983   7.39
6 1984   6.81




Plot


Code
avg_baseline <- arctic |> filter(year <= 1990) |> pull(extent) |> mean()
loss_pct     <- round((1 - min(arctic$extent) / avg_baseline) * 100)

col_fill   <- "#B3E5FC"
col_line   <- "#0277BD"
col_trend  <- "#C62828"
col_record <- "#E65100"
col_ref    <- "#78909C"
col_title  <- "#0D1B40"

records <- filter(arctic, year %in% c(2007, 2012, 2020))

ggplot(arctic, aes(x = year, y = extent)) +
  geom_area(fill = col_fill, alpha = 0.55) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = avg_baseline, linetype = "dotted",
             color = col_ref, linewidth = 0.7) +
  annotate("text", x = 1981, y = avg_baseline + 0.18,
           label = "1979-1990 mean", size = 2.9, color = col_ref, hjust = 0) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE,
              color = col_trend, fill = "#FFCDD2", alpha = 0.25,
              linewidth = 1.4, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_line(color = col_line, linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_point(data = records, color = col_record, fill = col_record,
             size = 4, shape = 21, stroke = 1.8) +
  annotate("segment", x = 2012, xend = 2012,
           y = min(arctic$extent), yend = min(arctic$extent) - 0.6,
           color = col_record, linewidth = 0.6) +
  annotate("text", x = 2012, y = min(arctic$extent) - 0.75,
           label = paste0("Record low\n", round(min(arctic$extent), 2),
                          " M km²  (", arctic$year[which.min(arctic$extent)], ")"),
           color = col_record, size = 2.9, fontface = "bold", hjust = 0.5) +
  annotate("text", x = max(arctic$year), y = max(arctic$extent) * 0.93,
           label = paste0("-", loss_pct, "% vs.\n1979-1990 avg"),
           color = col_trend, size = 4.5, fontface = "bold", hjust = 1) +
  labs(
    title    = "Arctic Sea Ice Is Melting",
    subtitle = "September minimum sea ice extent, 1979 to present",
    x        = NULL,
    y        = "Extent  (million km²)",
    caption  = "Source: NSIDC Sea Ice Index v4.0 | noaadata.apps.nsidc.org"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(1980, 2030, 5), expand = c(0.01, 0)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = function(x) paste0(x, " M")) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    plot.background  = element_rect(fill = "white", color = NA),
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = "#F0F8FF", color = NA),
    panel.grid.major = element_line(color = "gray88", linewidth = 0.35),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    plot.title       = element_text(face = "bold", size = 17, color = col_title),
    plot.subtitle    = element_text(size = 11, color = "gray45"),
    plot.caption     = element_text(size = 8, color = "gray60", hjust = 1),
    axis.text        = element_text(color = "gray40", size = 9),
    axis.title.y     = element_text(size = 10, color = "gray40", margin = margin(r = 8)),
    plot.margin      = margin(18, 18, 12, 18)
  )

title: Arctic Sea Ice Is Melting
text:
Part 2 — Maps (overview)

How the shapefiles work
NSIDC also publishes the sea ice boundary as a polygon shapefile for every month. We download and cache them locally, then read with sf.


Code
month_dirs <- c("01_Jan","02_Feb","03_Mar","04_Apr","05_May","06_Jun",
                "07_Jul","08_Aug","09_Sep","10_Oct","11_Nov","12_Dec")

fetch_ice_extent <- function(year, month = "09", pole = "N",
                             tmpdir = file.path(tempdir(), "nsidc_ice")) {
  dir.create(tmpdir, showWarnings = FALSE)
  mm       <- sprintf("%02d", as.integer(month))
  yymm     <- paste0(year, mm)
  pole_dir <- ifelse(pole == "N", "north", "south")
  mon_dir  <- month_dirs[as.integer(mm)]
  url <- paste0(
    "https://noaadata.apps.nsidc.org/NOAA/G02135/",
    pole_dir, "/monthly/shapefiles/shp_extent/", mon_dir, "/",
    "extent_", pole, "_", yymm, "_polygon_v4.0.zip"
  )
  zip_path <- file.path(tmpdir, paste0("ice_", pole, "_", yymm, ".zip"))
  if (!file.exists(zip_path) || file.size(zip_path) < 1000) {
    message("Downloading ", year, "-", mm, " ...")
    tryCatch(
      download.file(url, zip_path, quiet = TRUE, mode = "wb"),
      error = function(e) { message("  failed: ", e$message); return(NULL) }
    )
  }
  if (!file.exists(zip_path) || file.size(zip_path) < 1000) return(NULL)
  exdir <- file.path(tmpdir, paste0("ice_", pole, "_", yymm))
  suppressWarnings(unzip(zip_path, exdir = exdir, overwrite = FALSE))
  shp <- list.files(exdir, "\\.shp$", full.names = TRUE)[1]
  if (is.na(shp)) return(NULL)
  shape <- tryCatch(sf::st_read(shp, quiet = TRUE), error = function(e) NULL)
  if (is.null(shape)) return(NULL)
  shape$year <- year
  shape
}




Download shapefiles (every 5 years)


Code
years_overview <- c(1990, 1995, 2000, 2005, 2010, 2015, 2020, 2024)

ice_list <- lapply(years_overview, fetch_ice_extent, month = "09", pole = "N")
ice_list <- Filter(Negate(is.null), ice_list)
ice_all  <- do.call(rbind, ice_list)




Build the map


Code
world     <- ne_countries(scale = "medium", returnclass = "sf")
crs_polar <- "+proj=stere +lat_0=90 +lat_ts=70 +lon_0=0 +datum=WGS84 +units=m"

ice_proj   <- st_transform(ice_all,  crs_polar)
world_proj <- st_transform(world,    crs_polar)

clip_large <- st_buffer(
  st_sfc(st_point(c(0, 90)), crs = 4326) |> st_transform(crs_polar),
  dist = 1e7
)
world_clip <- st_intersection(world_proj, clip_large)

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = clip_large, fill = "#AED6F1", color = NA) +
  geom_sf(data = ice_proj,   fill = "white",  color = "white",   linewidth = 0.1) +
  geom_sf(data = world_clip, fill = "#8D6E63", color = "#6D4C41", linewidth = 0.15) +
  facet_wrap(~year, ncol = 4) +
  labs(
    title   = "Arctic Sea Ice Extent - September",
    caption = "Source: NSIDC Sea Ice Index v4.0"
  ) +
  theme_void(base_size = 10) +
  theme(
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = "#1A237E", color = NA),
    strip.text      = element_text(color = "white", face = "bold", size = 9),
    plot.title      = element_text(color = "white", face = "bold", size = 14,
                                   margin = margin(12, 0, 8, 12)),
    plot.caption    = element_text(color = "#546E7A", size = 7, hjust = 1,
                                   margin = margin(8, 12, 8, 0)),
    panel.spacing   = unit(0.4, "lines")
  )

title: Arctic Sea Ice Is Melting
text:
Part 3 — Maps (zoomed comparison)
Four key years in a closer view, with the actual extent area computed from the polygon geometry.


Code
years_zoom <- c(1985, 2000, 2012, 2024)

ice_zoom_list <- lapply(years_zoom, fetch_ice_extent, month = "09", pole = "N")
ice_zoom_list <- Filter(Negate(is.null), ice_zoom_list)
ice_zoom_all  <- do.call(rbind, ice_zoom_list)




Code
ice_zoom_proj <- st_transform(ice_zoom_all, crs_polar)

clip_tight <- st_buffer(
  st_sfc(st_point(c(0, 90)), crs = 4326) |> st_transform(crs_polar),
  dist = 5.5e6
)
world_clip_tight <- st_intersection(world_proj, clip_tight)
ice_zoom_clip    <- st_intersection(ice_zoom_proj, clip_tight)

# Compute area per year (million km²) from the actual geometry
ice_areas <- sapply(years_zoom, function(y) {
  sub <- ice_zoom_proj[ice_zoom_proj$year == y, ]
  if (nrow(sub) == 0) return(NA)
  as.numeric(sum(st_area(sub))) / 1e12
})
base_area <- ice_areas[1]

labels_df <- data.frame(
  year  = years_zoom,
  label = ifelse(seq_along(years_zoom) == 1,
                 sprintf("%.2f M km²\n(baseline)", ice_areas),
                 sprintf("%.2f M km²\n(-%.0f%% vs %d)",
                         ice_areas, (1 - ice_areas / base_area) * 100, years_zoom[1]))
)
ice_zoom_clip <- merge(ice_zoom_clip, labels_df, by = "year")

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = clip_tight,        fill = "#AED6F1", color = NA) +
  geom_sf(data = ice_zoom_clip,     fill = "white",   color = "#c8e0f0", linewidth = 0.15) +
  geom_sf(data = world_clip_tight,  fill = "#6D4C41", color = "#4E342E", linewidth = 0.2) +
  geom_sf_text(
    data = ice_zoom_clip |> group_by(year) |> slice(1),
    aes(label = label, geometry = geometry),
    stat = "sf_coordinates",
    color = "white", size = 3, fontface = "bold",
    nudge_x = -3.2e6, nudge_y = -4.0e6, hjust = 0
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~year, ncol = 4) +
  labs(
    title    = "Arctic Sea Ice Shrinkage - September Minimum",
    subtitle = "Polar stereographic projection, zoomed to 55N+",
    caption  = "Source: NSIDC Sea Ice Index v4.0"
  ) +
  theme_void(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = "#0D1B2A", color = NA),
    strip.text      = element_text(color = "white",  face = "bold", size = 12),
    plot.title      = element_text(color = "white",  face = "bold", size = 16,
                                   margin = margin(14, 0, 4, 14)),
    plot.subtitle   = element_text(color = "#90CAF9", size = 9,
                                   margin = margin(0, 0, 10, 14)),
    plot.caption    = element_text(color = "#546E7A", size = 7.5, hjust = 1,
                                   margin = margin(8, 14, 10, 0)),
    panel.spacing   = unit(0.8, "lines")
  )

title: EU Salary Race: Average Full-Time Adjusted Wages
text: Eurostat publishes yearly average full-time adjusted salaries (nama_10_fte) for every EU/EFTA country. This vignette pulls that series directly from the Eurostat API and turns it into three progressively more polished visualisations: an interactive time series, an animated bar chart, and a “bar chart race” — with Greece highlighted in red against the rest of Europe in gray.

title: EU Salary Race: Average Full-Time Adjusted Wages
text: Eurostat publishes yearly average full-time adjusted salaries (nama_10_fte) for every EU/EFTA country. This vignette pulls that series directly from the Eurostat API and turns it into three progressively more polished visualisations: an interactive time series, an animated bar chart, and a “bar chart race” — with Greece highlighted in red against the rest of Europe in gray.

title: EU Salary Race: Average Full-Time Adjusted Wages
text:
Packages


Code
# install.packages(c("dplyr", "tidyr", "countrycode", "plotly",
#                     "eurostat", "gganimate", "gifski", "scales", "ragg"))

library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(countrycode)  # geo codes -> country names / ISO codes
library(plotly)       # interactive charts
library(eurostat)     # Eurostat data API
library(gganimate)    # animation
library(gifski)       # GIF renderer
library(scales)       # axis formatting

title: EU Salary Race: Average Full-Time Adjusted Wages
text:
The data
get_eurostat() downloads the raw dataset table by its Eurostat code. We keep only country-level rows (dropping the EU27_2020 and EA20 aggregates), derive a plain-language country name and ISO code with countrycode, and rank countries by salary within each year.


Code
df_eusalary <- get_eurostat("nama_10_fte", filters = list(unit = "EUR"))
df_eusalary <- df_eusalary[!df_eusalary$geo %in% c("EU27_2020", "EA20"), ]

df_eusalary$year    <- lubridate::year(df_eusalary$time)
df_eusalary$country <- countrycode(df_eusalary$geo, origin = "eurostat", destination = "country.name")
df_eusalary$iso     <- countrycode(df_eusalary$geo, origin = "eurostat", destination = "iso2c")

df_eusalary$rank  <- NA
df_eusalary$color <- NA
for (i in unique(df_eusalary$year)) {
  df_eusalary[df_eusalary$year %in% i, "rank"] <-
    rank(-df_eusalary[df_eusalary$year %in% i, "values"], ties.method = "min")
}

df_eusalary[df_eusalary$country %in% "Greece", "color"]  <- "#E74C3C"
df_eusalary[!df_eusalary$country %in% "Greece", "color"] <- "gray70"

title <- "Average full time adjusted salary [nama_10_fte]"

head(df_eusalary[, c("country", "year", "values", "rank")], 12)


# A tibble: 12 × 4
   country  year values  rank
   <chr>   <dbl>  <int> <int>
 1 Belgium  1995  27855     3
 2 Belgium  1996  27875     3
 3 Belgium  1997  27774     3
 4 Belgium  1998  28200     3
 5 Belgium  1999  29691     3
 6 Belgium  2000  30506     4
 7 Belgium  2001  31777     3

 9 Belgium  2003  33678     3
10 Belgium  2004  34447     4
11 Belgium  2005  35009     4
